Uncertified DAG consensus, machine-checked

Protocols, properties and mechanisms, formalised in Lean 4
  • This talk presents a family of DAG-based consensus protocols in which blocks carry no certificates, and a formalisation of them in the proof assistant Lean 4 over its mathematics library Mathlib.
  • Every theorem cited in the deck is checked by the Lean kernel.
  • Whether the definitions state what the published papers mean has been checked only by human and LLM review, so the definitions should be read critically.
  • The background figure is a concrete DAG of 4 validators over rounds 0 to 5, taken from one of the witnesses used in the proofs.
Part I

Foundations

Scope

  • Protocols. Thirteen commit rules from the literature. Eleven are proved safe and to make progress, and seven of these also to include every reliable validator’s blocks. Two are shown unsafe or not live by counterexamples.
  • Properties. One small interface — four properties and a “support” — that each of the eleven rules is proved to satisfy.
  • Mechanisms. Chain quality, a storage bound, garbage collection, crash recovery, adaptive leaders and an adaptive leader count, checkpoints: each proved once against the interface, and composable. A pacemaker, proved for each rule, gives the liveness premise. Red Snapper, a fast path for owned objects, reads only the sequence of committed anchors.
  • Safety theorems use no assumption about the network.
  • The development has three parts: protocols, a common interface of properties, and mechanisms proved against that interface.
  • In the diagram the left arrow reads “each rule proves” the interface and the right arrow “each mechanism uses” it, so a mechanism proved once holds for every rule that satisfies the interface.
  • Of thirteen commit rules from the literature, eleven are proved safe and to make progress; seven of these are also proved to include the blocks of every reliable validator, and Nemo, FinWhale, Hydrozoan and Optimal-Hydrozoan have the progress result only.
  • The other two rules, Minnow and Black Marlin, are refuted by counterexample DAGs, and both counterexamples violate a safety property.
  • The mechanisms are chain quality, a storage bound, garbage collection, crash recovery, adaptive leaders, an adaptive leader count and checkpoints; a pacemaker, proved separately for each rule, supplies the premise that liveness needs, and Red Snapper uses only the sequence of committed anchors.
  • The safety theorems take no hypothesis about the network; the next slides define the problem and the model.

The problem: replicated agreement

  • n validators each keep a copy of one ordered log (a ledger).
  • Clients submit transactions to any validator.
  • Safety: no two correct validators output conflicting logs.
  • Liveness: every transaction from a correct client is eventually in every correct validator’s log.
  • Some validators may be faulty. The protocol must tolerate them without identifying them.
  • The problem is replicated agreement: n validators each maintain a copy of one ordered log of transactions.
  • In the diagram each row is a validator and each column a log position; v0, v1 and v2 hold tx₁, tx₂, tx₃, and the faulty v3 outputs tx₉ at position 2.
  • Safety requires that no two correct validators output conflicting logs; the output of a faulty validator such as v3 is unconstrained.
  • Liveness requires that every transaction submitted by a correct client eventually appears in the log of every correct validator.
  • This slide is background from the literature and is not itself a theorem; in the development the log is the sequence of committed leaders with their histories, and two validators' logs are proved in Lean to agree on every prefix of slots both have decided.
  • The protocol must tolerate faulty validators without knowing which they are; the next slide states how many.

Faults and quorums

  • A Byzantine validator may deviate arbitrarily from the protocol: send false messages, send none, or send different messages to different validators (equivocate).
  • A crashed validator stops and never resumes.
  • With n ≥ 3f + 1 validators, at most f Byzantine, a quorum is q = n − f validators.
  • Two quorums share at least n − 2f ≥ f + 1 validators, so at least one correct validator.
  • A correct validator does not equivocate, so two quorums cannot support two conflicting statements.
  • With n ≥ 3f + 1 validators and quorums of q = n − f, any two quorums share at least one correct validator.
  • A Byzantine validator may deviate arbitrarily, including equivocation, that is, sending different messages to different validators; a crashed validator stops permanently.
  • In the model f bounds the Byzantine validators only, and a crashed validator counts as correct; the liveness theorems name separately the validators that keep producing blocks.
  • The diagram has n = 4, f = 1: the quorums Q₁ = {v0, v1, v2} and Q₂ = {v1, v2, v3} share the shaded set {v1, v2}, of which v1 is Byzantine and v2 is correct.
  • In general |Q₁ ∩ Q₂| ≥ 2(n − f) − n = n − 2f ≥ f + 1, and at most f of those are Byzantine; this intersection property is proved in Lean and the safety arguments rest on it.
  • Since a correct validator does not equivocate, the shared correct validator prevents two quorums from supporting two conflicting statements.

What the network is assumed to do

  • Messages can be delayed arbitrarily, up to an unknown time GST (global stabilisation time).
  • A reliable validator is a correct one that keeps producing blocks. Liveness assumes a quorum of them.
  • After GST, what one reliable validator holds reaches every reliable validator within Δ. This is called view convergence.
  • Safety is proved with no assumption about the network.
  • Liveness is proved from view convergence and the protocol’s own rules.
  • Safety is proved with no assumption about the network; liveness assumes partial synchrony in the form of view convergence.
  • Partial synchrony is the standard model from the literature and is taken as background here: messages may be delayed arbitrarily until an unknown global stabilisation time GST.
  • In the diagram the two horizontal lines are the timelines of reliable validators w and v, and the arrows are messages; before the dashed line GST arrival times are arbitrary, after it each arrival falls in a shaded window of length Δ.
  • A reliable validator is a correct validator that keeps producing blocks, and liveness assumes a set of reliable validators of quorum size.
  • View convergence states that, for t ≥ GST and reliable v, w, every block w holds at time t is held by v at time t + Δ.
  • The liveness hypothesis also contains rules about how validators behave; these are part of the protocol, and the network contributes only view convergence.

Blocks and the DAG

  • Validators work in rounds. In each round each validator creates one block: a round number, its creator, references to earlier blocks, and a payload of transactions.
  • A valid block at round r > 0 references only blocks of round r − 1, at most one per creator, from at least n − f creators, its own creator among them.
  • The blocks and references form a directed acyclic graph (DAG). A block’s history is every block it reaches by references. A validator’s view is the set of blocks it holds, including their histories.
  • Blocks are named by identifier (a hash), so two validators may hold different sets of blocks but agree on what each identifier means.
  • The state of the protocol is a DAG of blocks, built round by round.
  • A block holds a round, a creator, references to earlier blocks and a payload; a block at round r > 0 is valid when it references only blocks of round r − 1, at most one per creator, from at least n − f creators, and includes a block by its own creator.
  • In the figure rows are validators and columns are rounds 0 to 2, with the Byzantine v0 shaded; block 8, by v0 at round 2, references blocks 4, 5, 6 of round 1, three creators, which meets n − f = 3, and block 4 is v0's own previous block.
  • The history of a block is every block it reaches by references, and a validator's view is the set of blocks it holds, which is closed under references.
  • Blocks are named by identifiers (hashes), so two validators may hold different sets of blocks while agreeing on the content of every identifier they share.
  • Some later rules change validity: Nemo uses a majority and drops the self-reference and distinct-creator conditions, FinWhale replaces the self-reference by an exclusion condition on leaders, and Bluestreak requires a quorum only of leader blocks.

Certified and uncertified DAGs

  • In a certified DAG (Narwhal, Bullshark), each block receives a certificate, built by an extra exchange of signatures, before others may reference it.
  • In an uncertified DAG (Mysticeti and this family), no certificate is sent.
  • A block two rounds above a leader is a certificate for it when its references include q = n − f votes for it, that is, blocks that reference the leader.
  • Every direct commit rule is then a threshold on a set of blocks found in the graph.
  • In an uncertified DAG a certificate is a pattern of blocks in the graph, so no extra message exchange is needed.
  • Panel (a) describes certified DAGs such as Narwhal and Bullshark, where n − f signatures on a block are aggregated into a separate certificate message before round r + 1 may reference it; this is background and is not formalised here.
  • In panel (b) rows are validators, columns rounds 0 to 2, and v0 is Byzantine; block 0 is the leader L, the three votes 4, 5, 6 reference it, and block 7 does not.
  • A vote for L is a block of round r + 1 that references L, and a certificate is a block of round r + 2 whose references include votes for L from q = n − f distinct creators.
  • Blocks 8, 9, 10 reference all three votes and are certificates, which is checked in Lean for block 8 on this DAG; block 11 references only the votes 5 and 6, so 2 votes is below q.
  • Each direct commit rule in the family is then a threshold on a set of blocks found in the graph; the next slide says which block is the leader.

Slots and the leader schedule

  • A slot k has a round and a leader. The schedule may put several leaders in one round and a leader in every round.
  • The candidates of slot k are the blocks of its leader at its round. A correct leader has at most one candidate; a Byzantine leader may have several.
  • Each slot is decided as commit (one candidate) or skip.
  • The ledger is the committed leaders in slot order, each followed by the blocks in its history not yet output.
  • Slots fix which validator's block is considered at which round and the order in which those blocks are decided.
  • A slot k has a round and a leader; in the table the top schedule has one leader per round rotating through v0 to v3, so slot k is at round k, and the bottom schedule has two leaders per round, slots 2r and 2r + 1.
  • The candidates of slot k are the blocks of its leader at its round; a correct leader has at most one, and an equivocating Byzantine leader may have several, which is checked on a concrete DAG with two candidates.
  • Each slot is decided as commit, which selects one candidate, or as skip.
  • The ledger lists the committed leader blocks in slot order, each followed by the blocks of its history that have not yet been output; the next slide gives the relation that decides a slot.

One decision relation for every rule

A slot is decided in one of four ways:

  1. Direct commit: the rule’s commit condition holds in the validator’s view.
  2. Direct skip: the rule’s skip condition holds.
  3. Indirect commit: a later committed slot (the anchor) links a candidate.
  4. Indirect skip: the anchor links no candidate.

The anchor is the nearest eligible committed slot above; every eligible slot in between must be skipped.

  • Every rule in the family uses one decision relation with four cases.
  • A direct commit or direct skip holds when the rule's commit or skip condition holds in the validator's view.
  • Otherwise the slot is decided from an anchor, a later committed slot j: j must be the nearest eligible committed slot above k, every eligible slot strictly between them must be skipped, and slot k commits a candidate that the anchor links, with a tie-break choosing among several, or is skipped when the anchor links none.
  • The flowchart orders the questions for presentation only: the relation is defined inductively, as four derivation rules, and a slot with no derivation is undecided.
  • For every rule satisfying the laws of the next slide it is proved in Lean that two validators who decide the same slot decide the same value, whether by direct or indirect cases.

A rule is a card of thresholds

Every rule fills in the same record:

  • the wave: how many rounds above the proposal the direct rules read;
  • the commit and skip conditions;
  • the link from an anchor, possibly in several graded rungs;
  • a tie-break between linked candidates.

Agreement and the agreement of ledgers are proved once, for every rule whose card satisfies a short list of laws.

  • Each rule is an instance of one record of parameters, and agreement is proved once for every instance that satisfies a short list of laws.
  • The fields are the wave, the number of rounds above the proposal that the direct rules read; the commit and skip conditions; the link from an anchor, possibly graded into rungs that are tried in order; and a tie-break between linked candidates.
  • The diagram shows the Mysticeti card in front: wave 2, commit on q certificates at r + 2, skip when q blocks at r + 1 reference no candidate, one rung that links L when the anchor's history contains a certificate for L, and no tie-break.
  • The cards behind it, Nemo-Nemo, Odontoceti, Hybrid and others, fill in the same five rows with different values.
  • From the laws it is proved in Lean that decisions agree between validators, that a decision persists as a view grows, and that the committed sequences and ledgers agree; slide 15 returns to the Mysticeti card.

Eligibility

  • An anchor at slot j is eligible for slot k when round(k) + wave < round(j).
  • A slot one round above k (5) cannot reach a certificate for k’s leader. A slot two rounds above (10) reaches one only if its own block is a certificate.
  • Anchoring at such slots would let one validator’s direct commit become another validator’s indirect skip.
  • An anchor at slot j is eligible for slot k only when round(k) + wave < round(j).
  • In the figure there is one leader per round, and the leader blocks 0, 5, 10, 15 sit at rounds r to r + 3; the badges evaluate the test with wave 2, which fails at r + 1 and r + 2 and holds at r + 3, and these three results are checked in Lean.
  • Certificates for slot k are blocks of round r + 2, so block 5 at r + 1 cannot reach one, and block 10 at r + 2 reaches only round r + 1 blocks besides itself, so it links slot k only if it is itself a certificate.
  • If such slots could anchor, a validator could indirectly skip slot k through an anchor that links nothing while another validator directly commits it; excluding them is the purpose of the condition.
  • The condition is upward-closed, so the nearest eligible committed slot is well defined.
  • The leaders of this schedule are drawn on a witness DAG for illustration; only the eligibility tests depend on the schedule.

A skip must count blocks

  • The absence of the leader’s block ? from a view is not a sound reason to skip: a validator cannot distinguish a silent leader from a leader whose block has not yet arrived.
  • In Mysticeti a direct skip needs n − f blocks of the round above that reference no candidate; each such block blames the slot. Those blocks exist, and later blocks do not alter them.
  • A direct skip must rest on a count of blocks that exist, and the absence of a block is not such a count.
  • Figure (1) shows a view that ends at round 5; slot 2 is at round 6 with leader v1, the dashed outline marks its block, which has not arrived, and no block of round 7 blames the slot, so the count is 0, below q.
  • A validator cannot distinguish a silent leader from a leader whose block is delayed; in Mysticeti a block blames a slot when it is in the round above the slot and references no candidate, and a direct skip needs n − f blaming blocks, which, once held, remain in every larger view with the same references.
  • It is proved in Lean that on this DAG, grown only to round 5, no view directly skips slot 2.
  • Step 1: figure (2) shows the same DAG grown to round 8: the leader block 25 has the four votes 28 to 31 and the four certificates 32 to 35, so slot 2 is directly committed, which is proved in Lean; a skip based on the absence at round 5 would have contradicted this commit.
  • Step 1: other rules skip differently, Nemo never directly and FinWhale, Hydrozoan and Bluestreak with other counts, and their slides give the details.

How the results are checked

  • Every definition and theorem is written in Lean 4 and checked by its kernel.
  • A witness is a small concrete DAG, usually 4 to 9 validators, on which Lean computes the verdicts. Witnesses show that hypotheses can be met and that bounds are tight; counterexamples show that a published claim fails.
  • Every DAG in this deck is drawn from a witness. Figures that are not are marked as diagrams.
def U3 : BlockUniverse (Fin 4) (Fin 12) Unit where
  ids := Finset.univ
  block := lk3   -- rounds 0, 1, 2
  complete := by decide
  valid := by decide
  no_equivocation := by decide

example : DirectCommit U3 0 0 := by decide

A DAG of 4 validators and rounds 0–2, and the statement that its block 0, at round 0, is directly committed.

  • Every definition and theorem is stated in Lean 4 and checked by its kernel, and every definition is tested on concrete DAGs called witnesses.
  • A witness is a small concrete DAG, usually of 4 to 9 validators, on which Lean computes the verdicts; witnesses show that hypotheses can be met and that bounds are tight, and counterexamples show that a published claim fails.
  • The code defines U3, 4 validators and 12 block identifiers over rounds 0 to 2; its last three fields, completeness of references, validity and absence of equivocation, are established by decide, meaning Lean evaluates them on the finite data.
  • The final line states that block 0 at round 0 is directly committed, and it too is established by evaluation.
  • The figure is the DAG of slide 7: the Byzantine row v0 is shaded, leader block 0 has the three votes 4, 5, 6 and the three certificates 8, 9, 10, and the commit badge marks slot 0, so the leader's being Byzantine does not prevent the commit.
  • Every DAG drawn in the deck comes from a witness, and figures that do not are labelled diagrams; Part II applies this setting to the individual protocols.
Part II

Protocols

The protocol family

Each rule in this part changes Mysticeti in one or more ways:

ChangeRules
Crash faults only, two roundsNemo-Nemo
A fast commit beside the slow oneFinWhale, Hydrozoan, Optimal-Hydrozoan
Fewer references per blockBluestreak
A larger committee, two roundsOdontoceti, Hybrid
No timing assumptionMahi-Mahi, Async BlueBottle, Steelhead

Then two published rules that have no indirect rule, Minnow and Black Marlin, with counterexamples to both; and a summary of all the rules.

  • This slide lists the rules of Part II; each rule changes Mysticeti in one or more ways, and the five bands group the rules by the kind of change.
  • In the figure an arrow joins a rule to a rule built on it, and its label names the change: for example, Odontoceti requires n ≥ 5f + 1, and Hybrid counts crash-prone validators apart from Byzantine ones.
  • Two of these relations are proved in Lean: Hybrid with fc = 0 has Odontoceti's thresholds, and Mahi-Mahi with a wave of w = 3 rounds is Mysticeti.
  • Steelhead is the composite of two rules, and Optimal-Hydrozoan uses Hydrozoan's committee.
  • After these rules come Minnow and Black Marlin, two published rules with no indirect rule, each with a counterexample, and then a summary of all the rules. We start with Mysticeti, on which every other rule in the figure is built.

Mysticeti

Faultsf Byzantine, n ≥ 3f + 1, quorum q = n − f
Round rthe leader proposes L
Round r + 1a block referencing L is a vote
Round r + 2a block referencing q votes is a certificate
Direct commitq certificates at r + 2
Direct skipq blocks at r + 1 reference no candidate
Indirecta certificate for L in the anchor's history; no tie-break
Commits at round r + 2 with no certificate messages. n = 3f + 1 validators tolerate f Byzantine faults.
Three rounds per commit; Odontoceti and Hybrid use two.
  • Mysticeti is the reference rule: every later rule in this part is described by how it differs from Mysticeti.
  • Each slot has a round r and a leader, whose block at round r is the candidate L. A round-r + 1 block that references L is a vote, and a round-r + 2 block that references q = n − f votes is a certificate.
  • Direct commit: q certificates at round r + 2. Direct skip: q blocks at round r + 1 reference no candidate of the slot; such a block is called a blame.
  • A slot with neither is decided by a later committed slot, the anchor: the slot is committed when the anchor's history holds a certificate for L, and skipped otherwise. No tie-break is needed, because two candidates of one slot that both have certificates are equal (proved in Lean).
  • Advantage: certificates are blocks of the DAG, so the rule sends no separate certificate messages, and n = 3f + 1 validators tolerate f Byzantine faults. Disadvantage: three rounds per commit, where Odontoceti and Hybrid use two.
  • That a commit takes three message delays, and that 3f + 1 is optimal for Byzantine faults, are claims from the literature, not theorems here.

Mysticeti: direct commit and direct skip

n = 4, f = 1, q = 3. Two candidates at round 0: v0's block 0 (L, slot 0) and v3's block 3.

  • At round 1, 4 5 6 are votes for 0; v3's block 7 does not reference it. 3 ≥ q
  • At round 2, 8 9 10 each reference those three votes: three certificates. 3 ≥ q: commit.
  • At round 1, 4 5 6 reference no block of v3 at round 0: three blames. 3 ≥ q: candidate 3 is skipped.
  • This slide applies the two direct rules to one DAG with n = 4, f = 1, q = 3.
  • Rows are validators and columns are rounds; the row of v0 is shaded as Byzantine. Brackets count blocks against q, and badges give the verdict on a candidate. The two candidates at round 0 are block 0 of v0, tagged L, and block 3 of v3.
  • Step 1: the round-1 blocks 4, 5, 6 reference block 0, so they are three votes, 3 ≥ q; block 7 of v3 does not reference block 0.
  • Step 2: the round-2 blocks 8, 9, 10 each reference the three votes 4, 5, 6, so each is a certificate. Three certificates reach q, and candidate 0 is committed directly.
  • Step 3: the same blocks 4, 5, 6 reference no round-0 block of v3, so they are three blames for candidate 3, and 3 ≥ q skips it directly.
  • A direct commit and a direct skip of the same candidate exclude each other (proved in Lean). The next slide shows a slot that neither direct rule decides.

Mysticeti: indirect commit

n = 4, f = 1, q = 3. Slots lie three rounds apart, all led by v0; slot 0's candidate is 0 (L).

  • At round 1, 4 5 6 are votes for L; 7 does not reference it, a blame.
  • At round 2 only v0's block 8 is a certificate for L. One certificate is fewer than q, and one blame is fewer than q: no direct decision.
  • The slot at round 3, led by v0 (12), is eligible. It is committed directly by rounds 4 and 5.
  • Its block references v0's certificate 8, so L is committed indirectly.
  • When a slot has fewer than q certificates and fewer than q blames, a later slot decides it; this slide shows an indirect commit.
  • In this DAG every slot is led by v0 and the slots lie three rounds apart. A slot is eligible as an anchor for the slot at round r when its round is at least r + 3; the anchor is the first eligible slot that is committed, provided every eligible slot before it is skipped.
  • Step 1: blocks 4, 5, 6 are votes for L, block 0; block 7 does not reference it and is a blame.
  • Step 2: only block 8 of v0 references the three votes, so slot 0 has one certificate and one blame, both fewer than q = 3, and no direct rule applies.
  • Step 3: the slot at round 3, with leader block 12, is eligible, and rounds 4 and 5 commit it directly, so block 12 is the anchor.
  • Step 4: the green path shows that block 12 references certificate 8, so the anchor's history holds a certificate for L, and L is committed indirectly.
  • An indirect skip cannot contradict a direct commit, because a direct commit puts a certificate in the history of every block from round r + 3 (proved in Lean). The next slide assembles these facts into the safety argument.

Mysticeti: why it is safe

  1. Two quorums share a correct validator.
  2. A correct validator votes once per round, so a slot has at most one certified candidate.
  3. A direct commit puts a certificate in every history from round r + 3.
  4. A direct skip leaves no certificate anywhere.
  5. So any two views decide every slot the same way, and their ledgers agree.

No step uses the network. Each rule on slides 19–44 is proved safe by the same five steps, with its own counts; the steps are the laws of slide 10.

  • Mysticeti's safety follows from five steps; the diagram shows what each step takes from the step before it.
  • Step 1 is quorum intersection: two sets of q = n − f validators share a correct validator when n ≥ 3f + 1. Step 2 follows because a correct validator votes for one block per round, so a slot has at most one candidate with a certificate.
  • Step 3: q certificates meet the q references of any later block, so a direct commit puts a certificate in every history from round r + 3. Step 4: q blames leave fewer than q votes, so a direct skip leaves no certificate anywhere.
  • Step 5: an anchor links at most one block, finds the certificate after a direct commit, and finds none after a direct skip. Hence any two views decide every slot the same way, and their ledgers agree; this is proved in Lean.
  • No step uses an assumption about the network. Each rule on the following slides is proved safe by the same five steps with its own counts.
  • For liveness, a backlog of undecided slots is decided by a run of consecutive committed slots (proved in Lean); with one slot per round, a run of three suffices.

Nemo-Nemo

Two rounds per commit; n = 2f + 1; safety holds for any number of crashes.
Crash faults only. A crashed leader's slot waits for an anchor. Liveness is proved when, beyond every slot, two consecutive slots have correct leaders.
  • Nemo-Nemo is Mysticeti for crash faults: a faulty validator may stop but never equivocates, and a commit takes two rounds instead of three.
  • Read the table row by row against Mysticeti: the committee is n ≥ 2f + 1, the quorum is a majority ⌊n/2⌋ + 1, and a majority of votes at round r + 1 commits directly, with no certificate round.
  • The rule has no direct skip, so a slot is skipped only indirectly. The indirect link needs one vote for the candidate in the anchor's history.
  • The reason given for the missing direct skip is that the implementation's skip quorum is the full stake, which is not reached once the leader has crashed; this is a reading of the implementation, not a theorem here.
  • Advantages: two rounds per commit, n = 2f + 1, and safety proved with no bound on the number of crashes. Disadvantages: crash faults only, and a crashed leader's slot waits for an anchor.
  • Liveness is proved when, beyond every slot, correct validators lead two adjacent slots; round-robin over 2f + 1 validators provides such a pair. The next slide shows both a crash and a schedule without such a pair.

Nemo-Nemo: the rules on a crash

n = 3, majority 2. Validator 2 creates blocks in rounds 0 and 1, then crashes.

  • Slot 3 (round 3, leader v0, 8): v0 and v1 vote at round 4. 2 ≥ 2: commit.
  • Slot 2 (round 2, leader v2) has no candidate. It has no direct skip; the anchor 11 at slot 4 links nothing for it: indirect skip. Slot 3 is not eligible for slot 2.
  • Lower figure: validator 2 has crashed before round 0 and leads every odd slot. The even slots commit; every odd slot stays undecided in every view. No two adjacent slots have live leaders.
  • This slide shows the Nemo-Nemo rules on a DAG with n = 3 and majority 2, in which validator 2 creates blocks in rounds 0 and 1 and then crashes.
  • Each round is one slot. An anchor for the slot at round r must lie at round r + 2 or later.
  • Step 1: slot 3 has leader v0 and candidate block 8; blocks 10 and 11 of v0 and v1 at round 4 vote for it, 2 ≥ 2, so it is committed directly. Slots 0, 1 and 4 also commit directly.
  • Step 2: slot 2 is led by v2, which has crashed, so it has no candidate and no direct decision. Slot 3 is not eligible for it; the anchor is block 11 at slot 4, whose shaded history holds no candidate for slot 2, so slot 2 is skipped indirectly.
  • Step 3: in the lower figure validator 2 has crashed before round 0 and leads every odd slot. The even slots commit directly; an odd slot k can be skipped only after the odd slot k + 2 is skipped, and the last odd slot has no anchor, so every odd slot stays undecided in every view (checked on this DAG).
  • In that schedule no two adjacent slots have correct leaders, which is the liveness hypothesis of the previous slide failing.

Odontoceti

MysticetiOdontoceti
Committeen ≥ 3f + 1n ≥ 5f + 1
Roundspropose, vote, certifypropose, vote
Direct commitn − f certificatesn − f votes
Direct skipn − f blamesn − f blames
Indirect linka certificate in historyn − 3f distinct voters in the anchor's history
Tie-breaknonethe least candidate
One round fewer per commit. Liveness needs two rounds of production instead of three.
Six validators to tolerate one fault, against four. Agreement depends on a fixed order of candidates.
  • Odontoceti removes Mysticeti's certificate round, so a commit takes two rounds; the committee grows to n ≥ 5f + 1.
  • Direct commit: n − f votes at round r + 1. Direct skip: n − f blames, as in Mysticeti.
  • Indirect link: the anchor's history must contain votes for the candidate from at least n − 3f distinct validators. Two candidates of a Byzantine leader can both pass this test, so the rule commits the least one; this is the tie-break row.
  • The direct rules are proved safe from n ≥ 3f + 1 alone; the bound n ≥ 5f + 1 is used only in the proofs about the indirect rule.
  • Advantages: one round fewer per commit, and liveness needs two rounds of block production instead of three. Disadvantages: six validators to tolerate one fault instead of four, and agreement depends on every validator using the same order on candidates.

Odontoceti: direct and indirect

n = 6, f = 1: direct threshold 5, indirect threshold 3. v0 is Byzantine.

  • Slot 0 (leader v0, 0): 5 blames, 5 ≥ 5: direct skip.
  • Slot 1: 3 votes, 3 blames: no direct decision. The anchor 21 at slot 3 has voters {1, 2, 3} in its history, 3 ≥ 3: indirect commit.
  • Slot 2: 2 votes, 4 blames: no direct decision. The anchor 28 at slot 4 has 2 voters in its history, 2 < 3: indirect skip.
  • This slide shows the three outcomes of Odontoceti's rules on one DAG with n = 6, f = 1: the direct threshold is n − f = 5, the indirect threshold n − 3f = 3, and v0 is Byzantine.
  • Each step marks one slot: its candidate tagged L, its votes and blames at the next round, and its anchor. The shaded region marks the voters in the anchor's history.
  • Step 1: slot 0's candidate, block 0, has the five blames 7 to 11, 5 ≥ 5, so slot 0 is skipped directly.
  • Step 2: slot 1's candidate, block 7, has the three votes 13, 14, 15 and three blames, neither reaching 5, so no direct rule applies.
  • Step 3: the anchor 21 at slot 3 has the voters {1, 2, 3} in its history, 3 ≥ 3, so slot 1 is committed indirectly.
  • Step 4: slot 2's candidate, block 14, has the two votes 20, 21 and four blames. The anchor 28 at slot 4 has two voters in its history, 2 < 3, so slot 2 is skipped indirectly.
  • The indirect rule agrees with the direct one because a direct commit is seen with at least n − 3f voters by every block from round r + 2 (proved in Lean).

Odontoceti: two twins pass

  • A Byzantine leader can make two blocks (twins, 0 and 6) in one round.
  • Both twins can reach the n − 3f threshold inside one anchor's history.
  • If each validator committed any passing twin, two validators could commit different twins.
  • The rule therefore commits the least passing candidate, an order every validator computes the same way. In the Hybrid figure both twins pass and the lesser, 16, is committed.
  • This slide explains Odontoceti's tie-break: a Byzantine leader can make two blocks in one round, called twins, and both can pass the indirect test.
  • Left figure, Odontoceti with n = 6: twins 0 and 6 each have three voters, 3 ≥ n − 3f, and the round-3 block 19 holds all six voters in its history (checked on this DAG). Block 19 is not the slot's committed anchor; at that anchor, block 15, only twin 0 passes.
  • If each validator committed any passing twin, two validators could commit different twins. The rule therefore commits the least passing candidate, in an order every validator computes the same way, and the linked candidate is then unique (proved in Lean).
  • The count is of distinct authors, so one validator's blocks count once.
  • Right figure, Hybrid with n = 9 and k = 4: twins 16 and 17 each have four voters in the history of anchor 27; the lesser, 16, is committed and 17 is refused (checked on a concrete DAG).
  • That the original thesis's argument picks "the" candidate without a tie-break is our reading of its text, not a theorem here. The next slide generalises Odontoceti to two kinds of faults.

Hybrid

  • fb Byzantine validators and fc crash-prone validators. A crash-prone validator never equivocates but may stop.
  • Quorum q = n − fb − fc. The rule is Odontoceti's: q votes to commit, q blames to skip, the least candidate with k voters in the anchor's history to link.
  • k must satisfy 2fb + fc + 1 ≤ k and k + 3fb + 2fc ≤ n. Such a k exists exactly when n ≥ 5fb + 3fc + 1.
  • With fc = 0 the thresholds are Odontoceti's.

Compared with Odontoceti: crash-prone validators are counted apart from Byzantine ones, which lowers the committee; the link threshold k becomes a parameter.
Tolerating one crash requires 4 validators; tolerating one Byzantine fault requires 6.
Crash-prone validators must not equivocate. When the fault sets are full, every correct validator is needed for liveness.
  • Hybrid generalises Odontoceti to two kinds of faults: fb Byzantine validators and fc crash-prone validators, which never equivocate but may stop.
  • The rule is Odontoceti's with quorum q = n − fb − fc: q votes commit, q blames skip, and the indirect link takes the least candidate with k voters in the anchor's history.
  • The link threshold k is admissible when 2fb + fc + 1 ≤ k and k + 3fb + 2fc ≤ n; an admissible k exists exactly when n ≥ 5fb + 3fc + 1 (proved in Lean). In the first table a dot marks an admissible k: only k = 2 at n = 4, and only k = 4 at n = 9.
  • With fc = 0 the thresholds are Odontoceti's, which is the case k = n − 3f (proved in Lean). The second table gives the smallest committee for each fault mix.
  • Advantage: one crash needs 4 validators, against 6 for one Byzantine fault. Disadvantages: that crash-prone validators do not equivocate is an assumption of the model; and when both fault sets are full the correct validators number exactly q, so every correct validator is needed for liveness.

Hybrid: the rules on four and five validators

  • fb = 0, fc = 1, n = 4, q = 3: validator 3 stops after round 0. Slot 1 (5) receives 3 votes: 3 ≥ q, a direct commit.
  • fb = 0, fc = 1, n = 5, q = 4, k ∈ {2, 3}: slot 1 (6) receives 2 votes and 3 blames, so no direct decision. Both voters are in the history of the anchor 18 at slot 3. At k = 2 slot 1 is committed; at k = 3 it is skipped.
  • This slide shows a direct commit of Hybrid under a crash, and an indirect decision that depends on the choice of k.
  • Upper figure: fb = 0, fc = 1, n = 4, q = 3, and validator 3 stops after round 0. Slot 1's candidate, block 5, receives the three votes 7, 8, 9, 3 ≥ q, and is committed directly. In this DAG the crashed validator's slot is not skipped directly.
  • Step 1: lower figure, n = 5, q = 4, admissible k ∈ {2, 3}, and no validator crashes. Slot 1's candidate, block 6, has the two votes 11, 12 and the three blames 10, 13, 14, so neither direct rule applies.
  • Step 2: the anchor 18 at slot 3 references the shaded blocks 11 to 14, so both voters are in its history.
  • Step 3: with k = 2 the two voters suffice and slot 1 is committed; with k = 3 they do not and slot 1 is skipped (both checked on this DAG). The difference comes from the references alone.
  • Both values of k are admissible, so each gives a safe rule, and on this DAG they decide slot 1 differently. The next slide shows a committee for which no k is admissible.

Hybrid: the committee bound is tight

With fb = 1, fc = 1 and n = 8 (one fewer than 5fb + 3fc + 1 = 9), no k is admissible. For every k, one full view of one DAG derives both a commit and a skip for the same slot.

candidate 1; anchor 17 (leader v1)voteblameanchorshaded row: Byzantine v0
  • This slide shows that the bound n ≥ 5fb + 3fc + 1 cannot be lowered: at fb = fc = 1 and n = 8, one fewer than 9, no k is admissible, and for every k one of two DAGs derives both a commit and a skip for one slot in one full view.
  • Both figures have the same layout: candidate 1 at round 0, its votes and blames at round 1, and the anchor 17 at round 2. Rows are grouped by vote and blame; the shaded row is the Byzantine v0, whose two round-1 blocks take opposite sides.
  • Here q = n − fb − fc = 6. First figure: six blames skip candidate 1 directly, while anchor 17 has three voters in its history, which commits the candidate for every k ≤ 3.
  • Second figure: six votes commit candidate 1 directly, while anchor 17 has three voters in its history, which skips the candidate for every k ≥ 4.
  • Together the two DAGs cover every k, so the bound is necessary (proved in Lean); with an admissible k the rule is safe, so the bound is also sufficient.

FinWhale

  • Committee n = 3f + 2p − 1, with 1 ≤ p ≤ f. Safety: up to f Byzantine. Fast path: when at most p are Byzantine.
  • Three thresholds: slow 2f + p, block validity n − f, fast n − p.
  • Fast commit at round r + 1: n − p votes.
  • Slow commit at round r + 2: 2f + p blocks, each referencing 2f + p votes.
  • Validity: if two of a block's references reference two different blocks of v, the block may not reference a block of v (leader exclusion).
  • p = 1 gives n = 3f + 1; p = f gives n = 5f − 1.
f = 2p = 1p = 2

Compared with Mysticeti: a second, faster commit rule at r + 1; the skip and the indirect rule also read "evidence" (slide 29); a different committee; leader exclusion instead of self-parent.
The parameter p sets both the committee size and the number of faults the fast path tolerates.
The committee grows with p. Beyond p faults only the slow path commits. Validity has no self-parent clause; the inclusion of every correct block is proved only for DAGs in which each block references its author's previous block.
  • FinWhale adds a fast commit at round r + 1 beside a slow commit at round r + 2; a parameter p with 1 ≤ p ≤ f sets the committee n = 3f + 2p − 1.
  • Safety holds with up to f Byzantine validators. After GST, the fast path commits when at most p validators are Byzantine (proved in Lean); with more faults, progress goes through the slow path.
  • Three thresholds: slow 2f + p, block validity n − f, and fast n − p. A fast commit needs n − p votes at round r + 1; a slow commit needs 2f + p blocks at round r + 2, each referencing 2f + p votes. The tables give n = 7 and n = 9 at f = 2, and the thresholds 6, 7, 7 at p = 2.
  • Validity uses leader exclusion: if two of a block's references reference two different blocks of a validator v, the block may not reference a block of v. Mysticeti's validity instead contains a self-parent clause, which requires a block to reference its author's previous block.
  • Compared with Mysticeti, FinWhale has a second commit rule, a skip and an indirect rule that also read evidence (slide 29), and a different committee: p = 1 gives n = 3f + 1, and p = f gives n = 5f − 1.
  • Advantage: one parameter sets both the committee and the number of faults the fast path tolerates. Disadvantages: the committee grows with p; beyond p faults only the slow path commits; and the paper's theorem that every correct block is included is proved only for DAGs in which each block references its author's previous block.

FinWhale: fast and slow commit

f = 2, p = 2, n = 9; validators 0 and 1 are Byzantine.

  • Fast. Seven round-1 blocks reference the leader's block 0: 7 ≥ 7, commit at round 1.
  • Slow. Every round-2 block references 7 votes; six such blocks suffice: 6 ≥ 6 certificates, commit at round 2.
leader blockvotecertificateshaded: six certificates counted
  • This slide shows both FinWhale commit rules on one DAG with f = p = 2 and n = 9; validators 0 and 1 are Byzantine.
  • Rows are the nine validators and columns are rounds 0 to 2; block 0 is the leader's block L. Brackets count against the fast threshold n − p = 7 and the slow threshold 2f + p = 6.
  • Step 1: the seven round-1 blocks 9 to 15 reference block 0, 7 ≥ 7, so block 0 is committed by the fast rule at round 1.
  • Step 2: every round-2 block references the seven votes and is therefore a slow certificate; the six shaded certificates suffice, 6 ≥ 6, so block 0 is also committed by the slow rule at round 2.
  • For the fast path, Lean proves a latency bound: after GST, with a correct leader and at most p Byzantine validators, every correct round-1 block is built within Δ + δ + 2·proc of its author entering round 0, where δ bounds the delivery of round-0 blocks and proc is the processing time. Reading this bound as two message delays is the paper's claim, not a theorem here.

FinWhale: skip and evidence

  • A round-r+2 block is evidence for l when it references at least f + p − 1 votes for l; if its references show the leader equivocating, at least f + p for l and at most f + p − 1 for every other candidate.
  • Direct skip: for every candidate, 2f + p blocks at r + 1 do not reference it, and 2f + p blocks at r + 2 are evidence for no candidate.
  • Indirect commit: the anchor's history holds a slow certificate for l, or 2f + p evidence blocks for l. The least such l is committed.
  • Evidence is needed because a fast commit may leave no slow certificate.
  • This slide defines evidence, which FinWhale's skip and indirect rules read in addition to certificates, and shows why it is needed.
  • A round-r + 2 block is evidence for l when it references at least f + p − 1 votes for l; if its references show the leader equivocating, it needs at least f + p votes for l and at most f + p − 1 for every other candidate.
  • First figure, f = p = 2: block 18 has seen both twins, with 4 votes for block 0 and 2 for twin 27, so it is evidence for 0 only. Block 19 has not seen the equivocation and references 5 votes, 5 ≥ 3. Block 20 has seen it and has 3 < 4 votes, so it is evidence for nothing.
  • Direct skip requires both that 2f + p round-r + 1 blocks omit every candidate and that 2f + p round-r + 2 blocks are evidence for no candidate. Indirect commit requires a slow certificate for l or 2f + p evidence blocks for l in the anchor's history; the least such l is committed.
  • Step 1: in the second figure the seven round-1 blocks 9 to 15 vote for block 0, 7 ≥ 7, a fast commit.
  • Step 2: each round-2 block references only five of these votes, 5 < 6, so no round-2 block is a slow certificate and there is no slow commit.
  • Step 3: every round-2 block is evidence for 0, and the anchor 30 has seven of them in its history, 7 ≥ 6, so it commits block 0 through evidence alone (checked on this DAG). A fast commit can leave no slow certificate, which is why the indirect rule reads evidence.

Hydrozoan

  • f Byzantine, c crashed, a slack k ≥ 0: n ≥ 3f + 2c + k + 1.
  • Thresholds: p = ⌊(c + k)/2⌋, q = n − f − c, qFast = n − p, qCert = ⌊(n + f)/2⌋ + 1, qSlow = 2f + c + 1, qWeak = f + p + 1.
  • Fast commit: qFast votes at r + 1. Slow commit: qSlow certificates at r + 2, each referencing qCert votes.
  • Skip: qFast blames at r + 1.
  • Indirect, two rungs: (1) a certificate in the anchor’s history; (2) if no candidate has one, the least candidate with qWeak votes in the anchor’s history.
  • Hydrozoan counts crash faults separately from Byzantine faults and adds a two-round fast path to a Mysticeti-style slow path.
  • The committee has f Byzantine validators, which may behave arbitrarily, c crashed validators, which follow the protocol until they halt and never equivocate, and a slack k ≥ 0, with n ≥ 3f + 2c + k + 1. The table gives each threshold at f = c = k = 1, n = 7.
  • Direct rules: a leader block is fast-committed when qFast round-r + 1 blocks vote for it; it is slow-committed when qSlow validators at round r + 2 each have a certificate, that is, a block referencing qCert votes for it; the slot is skipped when qFast round-r + 1 blocks blame it.
  • The indirect rule has two rungs. The anchor first looks for a certificate in its history; only when no candidate has one does it commit the least candidate with qWeak votes in its history. The second rung serves slots committed by the fast path alone, as the next slide shows.
  • Compared with Mysticeti: a crash fault adds 2 to the committee bound and a Byzantine fault adds 3, and the fast path commits in two rounds when at most p validators are actually faulty.
  • The liveness theorem proved in Lean guarantees the slow commit when a correct quorum, including the leader, is synchronised and fills the rounds of the wave. The two-round fast commit is a separate latency result, which needs every correct validator to take part and at most p actual faults.

Hydrozoan: why the second rung exists

n = 7; v0 is Byzantine and equivocates; v1 has crashed.

  • The leader 2 receives exactly qFast = 6 votes: fast commit.
  • No block is a certificate: each round-2 block references only 4 votes, one fewer than qCert = 5.
  • A validator that missed the fast commit consults the anchor 24. Rung 1 finds no certificate. Rung 2 finds 4 voters, at least qWeak = 3: commit.
  • A slot can be fast-committed while no certificate for it exists anywhere, so an indirect rule that looks only for certificates cannot recover that commit.
  • Rows are validators, reordered so that the Byzantine v0 and the crashed v1 are at the bottom; columns are rounds 0 to 3. Block 2, tagged L, is the leader block of slot 0; blocks 7 and 8 are the twins of the equivocating v0.
  • Step 1: blocks 7 and 9 to 13 vote for block 2, from six distinct validators, which is exactly qFast = 6: block 2 is fast-committed.
  • Step 2: each round-2 block references only 4 of these votes, one fewer than qCert = 5. Checked on this DAG: the set of certificates for block 2 is empty, so the slow path cannot fire.
  • Step 3: a validator whose view lacks vote 13 finds no fast commit, no slow commit and no skip. It consults anchor 24, slot 3's leader block: rung 1 finds no certificate, and rung 2 finds the 4 voters 9 to 12 (shaded) in the anchor's history, at least qWeak = 3, so it commits block 2, the verdict of the fast path.
  • The next slide states the inequality that guarantees rung 2 always finds qWeak votes of a fast commit.

Optimal-Hydrozoan

  • Hydrozoan’s committee, with at least one tolerated fault (f + c ≥ 1).
  • The fast path tolerates one more fault: pOpt = p + 1, qFastOpt = n − pOpt.
  • FinWhale’s evidence: a round-r+2 block is evidence for L when it references tPlain = n − (2f + c + pOpt) votes for L; or, if it saw the leader equivocate, tEquiv = f + pOpt votes with every rival below tEquiv.
  • Skip: qCert blames and qCert round-r+2 blocks that are evidence for nothing.
  • Indirect: (1) a certificate; (2) qCert evidence blocks in the anchor’s history. No tie-break.
  • Optimal-Hydrozoan lowers the fast quorum by one and replaces Hydrozoan's second rung by a count of evidence blocks, following FinWhale.
  • It keeps Hydrozoan's committee and assumes f + c ≥ 1. The fast path tolerates pOpt = p + 1 faults, with fast quorum qFastOpt = n − pOpt; the table shows that at n = 4, f = 1, Hydrozoan's fast path needs all 4 votes and this one needs 3.
  • A round-r + 2 block is evidence for the leader block L when it references at least tPlain votes for L. If it references votes for two different blocks of the leader, it has witnessed an equivocation, and it must then reference at least tEquiv votes for L and fewer than tEquiv for each rival, so it is evidence for at most one block.
  • Skip: qCert blames at round r + 1 and qCert round-r + 2 blocks that are evidence for no candidate. Indirect: rung 1 is a certificate, rung 2 is qCert evidence blocks in the anchor's history, and no tie-break is needed.
  • Advantages: one fewer vote on the fast path, and a skip proved to occur for every slot with no candidate once a correct quorum fills rounds r + 1 and r + 2. Disadvantages: the skip is decided one round later than Hydrozoan's; validity requires leader exclusion, that a block which has witnessed the leader's equivocation references no block of that leader; and for a slot with a candidate, a counterexample DAG shows that one Byzantine vote can prevent the skip.
  • That this fast path matches Hydrangea's lower bound is the paper's claim, not a theorem here.

Optimal-Hydrozoan: the evidence rung

n = 4; the leader v0 equivocates: copies 4, 5.

  • Copy 4 receives 3 votes: fast commit. No block is a certificate.
  • Each round-r+2 block sees both copies, references 2 votes for copy 4 and 1 for copy 5, and is evidence for copy 4.
  • The anchor’s history holds the three evidence blocks: rung 2 commits copy 4.
  • When the leader equivocates and no certificate exists, the evidence rung still commits the block the fast path committed.
  • n = 4; rows are validators, reordered; columns are rounds 0 to 4, with blocks 16 and 17 hidden. The leader v0 is Byzantine and has two blocks at round 1, copy 4 and its twin, copy 5.
  • Step 1: blocks 9, 10 and 12 vote for copy 4, from three validators, one of them v0 itself; this reaches qFastOpt = 3, so copy 4 is fast-committed. Block 11 votes for copy 5. Checked on this DAG: neither copy has a certificate.
  • Step 2: blocks 13, 14 and 15 at round 3 each reference votes 10, 11 and 12, so each sees both copies and has witnessed the equivocation. Each references 2 votes for copy 4, which is tEquiv = 2, and 1 for copy 5, below tEquiv: each is evidence for copy 4 alone. As leader exclusion requires, none of them references v0's block 9.
  • Step 3: anchor 18, slot 4's leader block, has the three evidence blocks in its history, from qCert = 3 validators, so rung 2 commits copy 4. This verdict is proved on this DAG.
  • The next protocol, Bluestreak, keeps Mysticeti's thresholds and changes the shape of the DAG.

Bluestreak

  • n ≥ 3f + 1, quorum n − f.
  • Sparse DAG: only leader blocks must reference n − f blocks. Other blocks reference their own previous block and, optionally, leader blocks.
  • A round-r+2 block claims L by naming it in its payload, or by referencing n − f votes for it.
  • Direct commit: n − f claims for a leader-tagged L.
  • Direct skip: n − f round-r+1 blocks in view, and for each candidate n − f of them that omit it.
  • Indirect: a claim for a tagged L in the anchor’s history.
Compared with Mysticeti: only leader blocks reference n − f blocks; a certificate is replaced by a claim, which only names the block.
Only leader blocks must reference n − f blocks, with the direct commit at r + 2 and n ≥ 3f + 1, as in Mysticeti.
Blocks need not reference a quorum, so chain quality is not shown. Claims require a discipline (slide 37).
  • Bluestreak keeps Mysticeti's committee and wave and makes the DAG sparse: only leader blocks reference a quorum.
  • Upper figure: Mysticeti at n = 4, every block references 3 blocks of the round below. Lower figure: Bluestreak at n = 4, rounds 0 to 3; the filled leader blocks reference 4 blocks, the others 1 or 2.
  • The format: a leader-tagged block references blocks of n − f distinct validators; an ordinary block references its own previous block and, optionally, leader blocks. The paper's design gives an ordinary block at most two references; that bound is the paper's statement, not a theorem here.
  • A round-r + 2 block claims L when it names L in its payload or references n − f votes for L. Direct commit: n − f claims for a leader-tagged L. Direct skip: n − f round-r + 1 blocks in view and, for each candidate, n − f of them that omit it. Indirect: one rung, a claim for a tagged L in the anchor's history, with no tie-break.
  • Compared with Mysticeti: the same bound n ≥ 3f + 1 and direct commit at r + 2 with far fewer references per block, and a claim, which only names a block, in place of a certificate.
  • Disadvantages: ordinary blocks reference no quorum, so the property that every block references a quorum is not shown and the chain-quality results of this deck do not apply; and because a claim is only a name, the proofs need a condition on anchors (slide 36) and a discipline on claims (slide 37).

Bluestreak: direct and indirect

n = 4, leader of slot k is v(k mod 4).

  • Slot 0 has 3 votes. Slots 1–3 are committed directly.
  • Slot 0 has only 2 claims (blocks 8 and 10), fewer than n − f = 3: not decided directly.
  • The anchor, block 15, references block 8, which claims block 0: slot 0 is committed indirectly.
  • On one DAG, three slots are committed directly and the fourth only through the indirect rule.
  • Rows are validators, reordered; columns are rounds; block ids are 4·round + creator, filled blocks are leader-tagged, and slot k is led by v(k mod 4). A claim arrow goes from the claiming block to the block it claims.
  • Step 1: blocks 4, 5 and 7 reference block 0, so slot 0's leader block has 3 votes, which is n − f: block 0 is certified. Slots 1, 2 and 3 each have 3 claims and are committed directly.
  • Step 2: slot 0 has only 2 claims at round 2. Block 8 names block 0 in its payload, and leader block 10 claims it by referencing the three votes 4, 5 and 7. Two is below n − f = 3, and the slot is not skipped either, so it has no direct verdict.
  • Step 3: the anchor is block 15, slot 3's committed leader block. Its history contains block 8, which claims block 0, so slot 0 is committed indirectly. Checked on this DAG, and by the agreement theorem every view that decides slot 0 decides block 0.
  • The anchor here is committed; the next slide shows that the indirect rule needs this.

Bluestreak: an anchor must be committed

  • A claim names a block; the votes behind it need not be in the claimer’s history.
  • Block 0 has one vote; blocks 5, 6, 7 omit it, and 3 ≥ n − f: slot 0 is skipped.
  • The Byzantine block 11 claims block 0, which has one vote.
  • So the indirect rule is safe only at a committed anchor, and block 15 is not certified. Every committed anchor is certified, backed and leader-tagged; the other rules in this deck place no condition on the anchor.
  • In Bluestreak the indirect rule is safe only at an anchor that is itself committed, because a claim can name a block that is not certified.
  • Rows are validators, reordered, with the Byzantine v3 second; block 0 is slot 0's leader block. Green marks a block that references block 0, red a block that omits it, and the dashed arrow a claim.
  • Step 1: only block 4 references block 0; blocks 5, 6 and 7 omit it, and 3 ≥ n − f, so slot 0 is skipped directly.
  • Step 2: the Byzantine block 11 names block 0 as certified in its payload, although block 0 has one vote. The claim discipline constrains only correct blocks, and this DAG satisfies it.
  • Step 3: block 15, slot 3's leader block, is eligible as an anchor for slot 0, and its history contains block 11's claim, so the indirect rule applied at block 15 would commit a slot already skipped. Block 15 is not certified, and in this DAG no block is committed.
  • Step 3: Bluestreak therefore requires an anchor to be certified, backed (every claim in its history names a certified block two rounds below the claimer) and leader-tagged. Proved in Lean: every committed anchor satisfies these three conditions. In the other protocols of this deck this anchor condition is trivially true.

Bluestreak: the claim discipline

  • From round 2, every claim in a correct block’s history must name a certified block exactly two rounds below the claimer.
  • Safety, liveness and every mechanism assume the discipline; garbage collection preserves it.
  • The claim discipline is the assumption on correct validators under which a claim may be relied on as a certificate.
  • Statement: from round 2 on, every claim in the history of a correct block names a block certified exactly two rounds below the claimer, where a block is certified when n − f validators reference it one round above.
  • Diagram: columns are rounds r − 1 to r + 2. Block B at r + 2 claims L at r, and three votes at r + 1 certify L; the shaded window holds everything a validator reads to check B's claim. A claim three rounds below, to L′, is not allowed.
  • Bluestreak's safety and liveness theorems and its mechanisms assume the discipline. Proved in Lean: an execution in which each correct validator builds only on blocks whose claims it has checked satisfies the discipline, and cutting the DAG at a garbage-collection horizon preserves it.
  • Because the check reads no round below r, it can still be made after older rounds are deleted. That the paper's unbounded reading of claims would make garbage collection impossible is an informal argument, not a theorem here.
  • The next protocol, Mahi-Mahi, changes the wave rather than the DAG.

Mahi-Mahi

  • n ≥ 3f + 1. A wave of w rounds: propose at r, vote at r + w − 2, certify at r + w − 1. At w = 3 this is Mysticeti.
  • A block votes for the least block by the leader at round r in its history (not only among its direct references).
  • Direct skip: n − f blames of the slot; a block blames the slot when its history holds no block of the slot.
  • The leader of a wave is revealed only after the wave, so the adversary cannot direct its message scheduling against it.
Compared with Mysticeti: a longer wave, votes found anywhere in the history, a skip per slot, and an unpredictable leader.
Live with no timing assumption about the network, given a schedule whose leaders include, in every window of slots, a validator whose block commits.
More rounds per commit; it needs an unpredictable leader, drawn by a common coin.
  • Mahi-Mahi lengthens Mysticeti's wave and reveals the leader only after the wave, so that the protocol stays live without timing assumptions.
  • A wave is the sequence of rounds from a slot's proposal to its decision. With wave length w, the leader proposes at r, votes are read at r + w − 2, and certificates, blocks that reference n − f votes, at r + w − 1. The diagram shows w = 5, with two propagation rounds; arrows point from a block into its history. At w = 3 the rule is proved to coincide with Mysticeti's.
  • A block votes for the least block of the leader at round r anywhere in its history. A block blames the slot when its history holds no block of the slot at all, and n − f blames skip the slot.
  • A common coin is a random value that the validators reveal jointly only after the wave; it names the leader, so the adversary cannot know the leader while it schedules messages. The coin is modelled only in the Steelhead part of the development; Mahi-Mahi's liveness theorem assumes instead that the leader schedule names a validator whose block commits in every window of slots, and concludes that some slot in every window commits.
  • Proved in Lean: safety for every w ≥ 2, liveness for w ≥ 4. The advantage is liveness under asynchrony; the disadvantages are more rounds per commit and the need for an unpredictable leader.

Mahi-Mahi: votes and what a wave commits

  • At w ≥ 4 a history can contain two twins of the leader; a block votes only for the least.
  • At w ≥ 4, once a correct quorum has blocks at rounds r + 2 and r + w − 1, some correct validator’s round-r block is directly committed.
  • At w ≥ 5, at least n − f − b correct validators are good: their block would commit if chosen (b = number of Byzantine).
  • An adversary that knows the leader in advance can prevent the leader’s block from entering the other validators’ histories.
  • twin4: twins 0 and 4 lie in block 8’s history; 8 votes for 0.
  • aim4: block 5 enters no other history up to round 3. Good at w = 4: {0, 2, 3} (shaded); at w = 5: all.
leader blockvoteblame
  • Reading votes through the whole history has two consequences: a history can contain twins, and enough validators are good.
  • Left figure: the Byzantine v0 has twins 0 and 4; both lie in block 8's history (the path 8 → 5 → 0 is drawn), and block 8 votes for the least, 0. Checked on this DAG.
  • A validator is good for round r when its round-r block would be directly committed if it were chosen as leader. Proved: at w ≥ 4, if a correct quorum has blocks at rounds r + 2 and r + w − 1, some correct validator is good; at w ≥ 5, with blocks at r + 3 and r + w − 1, at least n − f − b correct validators are good, where b is the actual number of Byzantine validators.
  • Right figure, rounds 1 to 3: v1's leader block 5 enters no other validator's history up to round 3. Block 13 votes for it and blocks 12, 14 and 15 blame the slot: skipped at w = 4, committed at w = 5. The good validators are {0, 2, 3} (shaded) at w = 4 and all four at w = 5.
  • On this DAG a fair round-robin schedule, which the adversary knows in advance, violates the unpredictability assumption at w = 4: the adversary keeps the leader's block out of other histories. This is why Mahi-Mahi draws the leader by a coin after the wave.

Async BlueBottle

  • n ≥ 5f + 1. Propose at r; vote and decide at r + 2, with votes found in the history as in Mahi-Mahi; no certificates.
  • Direct commit: n − f votes. Direct skip: n − f blames.
  • Indirect: n − 3f voters in the anchor’s history; the least passing candidate is committed.
  • The leader is unpredictable, as in Mahi-Mahi.
Compared with Odontoceti: the vote round moves from r + 1 to r + 2 and votes are found anywhere in the history, so that the rule is live with an unpredictable leader.
Live with no timing assumption (given such a schedule, slide 38), three rounds per wave; commit probability at least (n − 3f)/n per wave.
Five validators per fault (n ≥ 5f + 1), against three for Mahi-Mahi, and an unpredictable leader.
  • Async BlueBottle uses Mahi-Mahi's history-based vote and unpredictable leader with Odontoceti's committee n ≥ 5f + 1, in a three-round wave without certificates.
  • The leader proposes at r; at r + 2 each block votes, and the direct rules count those votes, so no certificate round is needed.
  • Diagram, n = 6, rounds r to r + 2: the shaded region is the history of v0's round-r + 2 block B. B references n − f = 5 round-r + 1 blocks, one of which references L, so L is in B's history and B votes for it.
  • Direct commit: n − f votes; direct skip: n − f blames of the slot. Indirect: at least n − 3f distinct validators whose votes for L lie in the anchor's history; when several candidates pass, the least is committed.
  • Compared with Odontoceti, the vote moves from r + 1 to r + 2 and is read through the whole history, so that the rule is live with an unpredictable leader. Advantages: three rounds per wave, at least n − 3f good correct validators, and a proved commit probability per wave of at least (n − 3f)/n. Disadvantages: five validators per fault against three for Mahi-Mahi, and the coin.
  • Safety is proved, and liveness under the unpredictability assumption; the property that a slot without support is skipped is not established for this rule.

Async BlueBottle: witnesses

  • n = 6, a fair schedule, a leader known in advance: block 1 enters only v1’s history; five blames: direct skip.
  • Two twins, 0 and 6, can both pass the n − 3f test at one anchor: the least must be chosen.
  • The paper’s procedure skips per candidate, which can skip one twin while the other is committed.
leader block; 0 and 6 are twins of v0vote, for the least twin in its historyblamea vote’s path to the leader block
  • Three concrete DAGs at n = 6 show why the leader must be unpredictable, why the indirect rule needs a tie-break, and why the skip is per slot.
  • Left: slot 0 is led by v1, whose block 1 enters only v1's history; block 13 votes for it (path 13 → 7 → 1) and blocks 12 and 14 to 17 blame the slot, five blames, which is n − f: a direct skip. The round-robin schedule is proved fair, and on this DAG it violates the unpredictability assumption; liveness therefore rests on unpredictability rather than on fairness.
  • Middle: v0's twins 0 and 6; blocks 13 to 15 vote for 0 and blocks 16 to 18 for 6. Block 19 sees all six votes, 3 for each twin, and n − 3f = 3, so both twins pass the indirect test at block 19, and the rule must choose the least. At this DAG's anchor, slot 3's block 22, only twin 0 passes, and slot 0 commits block 0; both facts are proved on this DAG.
  • Right: every round-2 history holds both twins and every block votes for the least, so twin 0 has 6 votes and is committed directly. Under the paper's per-candidate skip, twin 6 has n − f non-voters, so the paper's procedure returns a skip if it examines twin 6 before twin 0. The slot-level blame used here has no blamer, and the slot commits.
  • Steelhead, next, combines a synchronous and an asynchronous rule on one DAG.

Steelhead

  • Each slot has a kind: synchronous (a known leader, short wave ws) or asynchronous (an unpredictable leader, long wave wa).
  • A slot is decided by the rule of its kind, at its own wave; its anchor lies at or above round + w(kind).
  • A period P sets the kinds: round r is asynchronous when r mod P = 0. The period is adapted at intervals of I rounds.
  • Two instances: Mysticeti with Mahi-Mahi (n ≥ 3f + 1, waves 3 and wa ≥ 4), and Odontoceti with Async BlueBottle (n ≥ 5f + 1, waves 2 and 3).
Compared with Mysticeti: two rules on one DAG, chosen per slot, and a controller that chooses how often the asynchronous rule runs.
Short waves while the network is synchronous; liveness under asynchrony.
Two rules, a coin, a period controller, and a failover (slide 44).
  • Steelhead runs two rules on one DAG and chooses per slot which of them decides it.
  • Each slot has a kind: synchronous, with a leader known in advance and a short wave ws, or asynchronous, with a leader drawn by the coin and a long wave wa. The period P sets the kinds: round r is asynchronous exactly when r mod P = 0, and P is changed once per interval of I rounds.
  • Diagram at P = 3, ws = 3, wa = 5: the top row gives rounds 0 to 6 and their kinds. Slot 0 is asynchronous, its wave spans 5 rounds and its anchor lies at round 5 or above; slots 1 and 2 are synchronous, with anchors at or above rounds 4 and 5. Each slot's anchor floor is its round plus the wave of its own kind.
  • Reading the floor at ws for every slot is unsafe: on a counterexample DAG, one view derives both a commit and a skip for an asynchronous slot.
  • Two instances are formalised: Mysticeti with Mahi-Mahi (n ≥ 3f + 1, waves 3 and wa ≥ 4) and Odontoceti with Async BlueBottle (n ≥ 5f + 1, waves 2 and 3). The rule that updates the period is a parameter of the proofs; the paper's update rule is modelled as one instance.
  • Advantages: short waves while the network is synchronous, and liveness under asynchrony. Disadvantages: two rules, a coin, a period controller, and a failover, which slide 44 presents.

Steelhead: the stall

  • At any period P ≥ ws, an adversary delivers each synchronous leader’s block to exactly f + 1 validators. Neither a commit nor a skip quorum forms.
  • The synchronous slot just below each asynchronous round is then undecided in every view, and the output does not advance beyond it.
  • The asynchronous slot 0 is committed: round 4 certifies block 1. Slot 3 stays undecided whatever slots 0 and 4 decide.
  • At period 1 every slot is proved to be decided.
  • With a fixed period above 1, an adversary can keep Steelhead's output from advancing.
  • n = 4, period 4, ws = 3, v0 Byzantine: rounds 0 and 4 are asynchronous, rounds 1 to 3 synchronous, and the leader blocks are 1, 6, 11 and 12.
  • Step 1: each synchronous leader block is referenced by 2 blocks of the next round and omitted by the other 2, since the adversary delivers it to f + 1 = 2 validators. Both counts are below n − f = 3, so neither a certificate nor a skip quorum forms.
  • Step 2: the theorem, proved in Lean for every period P ≥ ws: if no synchronous candidate is certified and no synchronous slot is skipped directly, no slot at a round congruent to P − 1 mod P is decided in any view. Here that is slot 3, and the output does not advance beyond it.
  • Step 3: the asynchronous slot 0 is committed, since at wave 5 all four round-4 blocks certify block 1; slot 3 stays undecided whatever slots 0 and 4 decide. At period 1 every slot is proved to be decided, under the unpredictability assumption on the coin. For the Mysticeti and Mahi-Mahi pair, ws = 3, so period 2 is covered by neither result.
  • Steelhead therefore needs a way to return to period 1, which is the failover on the next slide.

Steelhead: control and failover

  • The period is changed by a second verdict, read at the asynchronous control slots of each interval.
  • Failover: when the anchor is more than I rounds above the last committed output, the next interval runs at period 1.
  • Under failover a stalled slot is decided almost surely. The probability it is still undecided after M blocks, each of wa·K coins, is at most 2 · ((nwa·K − (n − f − b)wa·K) / nwa·K)⌊M/2⌋, where b is the number of Byzantine validators and K bounds the period.
  • The period of each interval is chosen by the asynchronous rule, and a failover to period 1 makes a stalled slot decided with probability 1.
  • At the asynchronous control slots of each interval, a second verdict, of the asynchronous rule, selects an anchor, and the period of the next interval is computed at that anchor. Failover: when the anchor lies more than I rounds above the round of the last committed output, the next interval runs at period 1; proved in Lean.
  • Figure, I = 8: the period row gives the periods 4, 4, 1, 1 of four intervals; the anchor row gives anchors at rounds 4, 12 and 17. In interval 1 of the table, the second column, the anchor is at round 12, the last commit at round 0, and 0 + 8 < 12: failover. In interval 3, the fourth column, the coin names committed candidates at rounds 25 to 29, and slot 3 is decided in a view holding round 33.
  • The figure is checked on a concrete DAG: the stalling DAG of the previous slide, extended, with the coin naming validator 2 at every round.
  • Under failover, the probability that a stalled slot is still undecided after M blocks of wa·K coins each is at most the bound on the slide, where b is the actual number of Byzantine validators and K bounds the period. The base is the probability that a block of wa·K coins names some validator that is not good; the bound tends to 0, and the slot is decided almost surely.
  • These results assume wa ≥ 5, K ≤ I, wa ≤ I and wa·K ≤ q·I for a whole number q: the blocks begin q intervals apart, so each block of wa·K rounds ends before the next begins.

Minnow: the rule

  • n ≥ 3f + 1; no self-parent rule.
  • Commit a leader block l when n − f processes reference it from the round above, and every earlier leader slot is resolved: one of its blocks is in l's history, or is concurrent with l and committed or skipped.
  • Skip when n − f processes of the round above have no block that references it.
  • The rule consults no later anchor.
  • This slide states Minnow's commit and skip conditions; the next two slides refute the rule's safety and its liveness.
  • In the diagram, the three outlined blocks of round r + 1 are n − f processes that reference the leader block l; the two green boxes on the left are the two ways in which an earlier leader slot can be resolved.
  • An earlier slot is resolved for l when some block of that slot is in l's history, or is concurrent with l (neither block is in the other's history) and is itself committed or skipped. The condition asks for some block of the slot, which need not be the block that is committed.
  • A skip counts processes: n − f processes of round r + 1 none of whose blocks references the leader block. If the skip counted blocks instead, one block could be committed and skipped at once; this is checked on a concrete DAG.
  • Minnow has no self-parent rule, and its commit rule reads only the round above the leader and the earlier slots; it consults no later anchor. The next slide shows what the existential over a slot's blocks permits when a leader equivocates.

Minnow: an earlier leader committed after a later one

n = 4. Process 0 equivocates at round 0: blocks 0 and 4. Block 4 is referenced by process 1 only.

  • A validator missing block 5 sees the round-1 leader block 6 reach block 4, which resolves slot 0. Block 6 is committed, while slot 0 is still undecided.
  • Blocks 5 and 12 arrive. Block 0 now has a quorum and is committed for slot 0, after the later leader.
  • Under Minnow, one validator commits the round-1 leader while slot 0 is undecided, and in the full DAG a block is then committed for slot 0, after the later leader.
  • Initial state: n = 4, and process 0 is Byzantine. Blocks 0 and 4, outlined in red, are twins: two blocks of process 0 in slot (0, 0), the first leader slot. Only process 1 references block 4.
  • Step 1: this validator's view lacks blocks 5 and 12. Block 0 has two references (bracket 2 < q = 3), and only one process does not reference it, so slot 0 is neither committed nor skipped. The round-1 leader block 6 reaches block 4 (green path), which resolves slot 0, and block 6 has three references, so block 6 is committed.
  • Step 2: with blocks 5 and 12 present, block 0 is referenced by processes 0, 2 and 3 and is committed for slot 0, after block 6 was committed. Block 4 never has a quorum, so it is never committed. Both views are checked on this DAG in Lean.
  • This violates the paper's Safe-Commit property: the first validator has output block 6 with slot 0 undecided, and no extension of its output places block 0 before block 6.
  • The published proof assumes that the block resolving the earlier slot is the block that could be committed. Here the slot holds two blocks: block 0 can be committed and is outside block 6's history, while block 4, in block 6's history, can never be committed. The next slide turns to liveness.

Minnow: slots that are never decided

  • Under Minnow a slot can remain undecided in every view, and such a slot prevents the commit of every later leader whose history lacks it.
  • Initial state, left figure: n = 4, f = 1, process 0 Byzantine, two leaders per round in round robin. Process 0 sends each block to process 1 only, so each of its leader blocks has two references (bracket 2 refs < 3) and two non-references (bracket 2 non-refs < 3): too few to commit and too few to skip. Every round holds all four blocks, so neither count can change.
  • The second leader of round 0 is concurrent with block 0, and the two leaders of round 1 are processes 2 and 3, which did not reference it; so none of them can resolve slot 0. From round 2 on, block 0 is in every leader's history, but by then process 0 leads again. Proved in Lean: none of the first ten leader slots of this DAG is committed.
  • Step 1: the right figure shows a simpler attack. Process v0 issues no blocks, so its slots at rounds 0 and 2 hold no block (dashed). The rule asks for some block of the slot, so an empty slot is never resolved and no later leader is committed. Rounds still advance, because n − f = 3 blocks complete a round.
  • Step 2: the same DAG with one leader per round. Leader block 11 at round 2 reaches blocks 0 and 6 (green paths) and is committed, while slots 0 and 1 remain undecided. The commit uses the history condition, the condition that the previous slide showed to be unsafe when a slot holds two blocks.
  • The gap could be closed only by lowering the skip threshold below 2f + 1. That 2f + 1 is the least safe skip threshold is argued, not proved here; present it as a claim.

Black Marlin: the rule

  • n ≥ 3f + 1; one anchor per round; no certificates.
  • Commit an anchor B at round r when n − f validators reference it at round r + 1, and some anchor at r + 1 references B and is itself referenced by n − f validators at r + 2.
  • There is no skip. Anchors that are not committed are output through a descent from a later committed anchor.
  • This slide states Black Marlin's commit rule: an anchor is committed by two consecutive quorums, without certificates and without a skip.
  • In the diagram, B is the anchor of round r. The outlined group of round r + 1 is n − f blocks that reference B, among them the anchor A (arrow labelled link); the outlined group of round r + 2 is n − f blocks that reference A.
  • An anchor of round r is a block of that round by the validator that the rotation elects for it; an equivocating validator may have several. B is supported when n − f distinct validators reference it from round r + 1, linked when a supported anchor of round r + 1 references it, and committed when it is both.
  • There is no skip. From a committed anchor the descent moves to an anchor of the highest round in its history, choosing the anchor whose history has an anchor in the nearest round below it, and then the least identifier, and outputs the blocks below each anchor it visits.
  • The paper describes the rule as needing no reliable broadcast and no common coin; this is the paper's description, not a proved statement here. Black Marlin is not an instance of the properties interface of Part III. The next slide shows that its agreement fails.

Black Marlin: agreement fails

n = 4, f = 1. Validator 0 equivocates at round 2: blocks 8 and 12.

  • Block 8 is committed; block 12 is not supported.
  • The committed anchor 19 at round 4 omits block 14.
  • One validator outputs block 8 for round 2; another outputs block 12.

Total order also fails, on blocks 5 and 7 of correct validators.

  • Two correct validators following Black Marlin output different blocks for round 2, so agreement fails; total order fails as well.
  • Initial state: n = 4, f = 1, row v0 Byzantine. The rotation elects validator 0 at round 2, and it issues two anchors there, the twins 8 and 12 (red outline).
  • Step 1: blocks 14, 15 and 16 reference block 8 (bracket 3 ≥ q), and the round-3 anchor 14 references block 8 and is referenced by blocks 17, 18 and 20; so block 8 is committed. Block 12 is referenced by block 13 only (bracket 1 < q) and is not supported. Proved in Lean: at most one anchor of a round is supported, so the commit rule alone commits one twin.
