  • Step 2: the round-4 anchor 19 omits block 14, which is valid since a block needs n − f = 3 references, and block 19 is committed. A validator whose view lacked blocks 17, 18 and 20 at round 4 saw block 14 unsupported and did not commit block 8; it commits block 19 later. Its descent from block 19 finds no round-3 anchor, meets both twins at round 2, and its choice prefers block 12 (green path through 13).
  • Step 2: so one validator outputs block 8 for round 2 and the other outputs block 12; each output drops a second block of the same author and round, so neither validator ever outputs the other's twin. This is checked on the concrete DAG.
  • Step 2: total order fails on blocks 5 and 7 of correct validators, neither of which has a twin: the two validators output them in opposite orders, because block 5 is below block 8 and block 7 below block 12. A different rule for choosing among twins does not repair this. The commit rule's uniqueness and ordering lemmas are proved in Lean; the failure lies in the descent.

Every rule on one page

  • The table compares the thirteen rules of Part II, eleven proved and two refuted, on fault model, committee size, latency, indirect rule, tie-break and leader schedule.
  • Columns: Faults is the fault model; Committee is the required number of validators n; Rounds to commit counts the leader's round and the rounds of the blocks that commit it directly, one more than the rule's wave length.
  • Indirect rungs is the number of indirect steps and the evidence each reads; Tie-break says whether, when two twins pass a test, the least is chosen; Leader says whether leaders are scheduled in advance or unpredictable.
  • Odontoceti, Hybrid and Async BlueBottle require n ≥ 5f + 1 or its hybrid analogue, and the first two commit in two rounds. FinWhale and Hydrozoan have a two-round fast path and a three-round slow path.
  • For Hybrid, n ≥ 5fb + 3fc + 1 is the bound at which an admissible voter threshold k exists; the fault model alone asks only n ≥ 3(fb + fc) + 1.
  • For Minnow and Black Marlin the rounds are those their commit rules read; neither has an indirect rule. The next slide lists what the formalisation found for each rule.

What the formalisation found

  • This table collects, rule by rule, the defects and corrections that the formalisation found; each is proved in Lean or shown by a concrete DAG.
  • Twins: in Odontoceti, Hybrid and Async BlueBottle two twins can both pass the indirect test, so the rule must choose the least by an order every validator computes.
  • Published proofs: FinWhale's Lemma 22 counts a window that is a full leader cycle plus two rounds only when p ≤ 1; the lemma holds for every p by a pigeonhole argument, and Lemmas 18/19 and 6/7 are proved by other routes. Hydrozoan's six inequalities hold without the slack cap, and the agreement proof needs inequality 6 with an extra − f.
  • Counts and probabilities: Mahi-Mahi's good validators number n − f − b, because twins of Byzantine leaders can split votes; the proved commit probability per wave is at least (n − f − b)/n, never below 1/3. In Steelhead's timeout appendix one probability is f/n, not (n − f)/n.
  • Rule changes: Bluestreak's indirect rule needs a committed anchor and claims read two rounds deep; Steelhead's period update can keep a stalled period, so liveness needs the failover, with intervals I ≥ 2K and I ≥ K + wa − 2. The adaptive leader count's health test passes vacuously when the interval is shorter than the wave.
  • Minnow and Black Marlin are refuted by the counterexamples of slides 45–49.
  • Three lessons recur: fix an order wherever two twins can pass a test; count blocks that exist instead of inferring from absence; decide indirectly from a later committed anchor.
Part III

Properties

From rules to properties

Mechanisms such as garbage collection or crash recovery should not be proved once per rule. Instead:

  • each rule is proved to have a few properties;
  • each mechanism is proved once, using only those properties.

Eleven rules (all but Minnow and Black Marlin) have the properties.

  • Part III introduces an interface of properties, so that each mechanism is proved once for all eleven rules.
  • In the diagram, the rules on the left each prove the properties in the middle box, and the mechanisms on the right are each proved from the properties alone.
  • With this division, a new rule requires proofs of the properties only, and a new mechanism requires a proof from the properties only.
  • Minnow and Black Marlin are excluded: the previous slides refute them, and neither is given the properties.
  • Slide 2 shows the same three layers and lists the eleven rules. The next slide defines what a mechanism may read of a rule.

The carrier

A mechanism accesses a rule only through its carrier:

  • a type of universes (all blocks) and of views (what one validator holds);
  • the round, creator and references of each block;
  • the decision relation: under schedule S, view V decides slot k as v.

Laws: a view holds only universe blocks; a view holds every block that its blocks reference; references go one round down.

  • The carrier is the interface between rules and mechanisms: it is all that a mechanism may read of a rule.
  • In the diagram, the outer box is the universe, the set of all blocks; the blue box is one view, the blocks one validator holds; the dashed round-3 blocks are in the universe and outside the view. Every reference goes one round down.
  • The carrier gives the round, creator and references of each block, and the decision relation, drawn at the bottom: under a schedule S, which assigns each slot a round, a leader and a kind, view V decides slot k as a block L (commit) or as none (skip).
  • The decision relation is a relation, so a view may leave a slot undecided. Three laws hold for every rule: a view holds only universe blocks, a view holds every block its blocks reference, and each reference goes one round down.
  • The eleven rules are given carriers (slide 2). The next slides state the properties of the decision relation.

Banded: a verdict reads a finite band of rounds

Each verdict depends only on the blocks in a band of rounds, from the slot's round to some round top. Any other universe, view and schedule that match in the band — up to a shift of round and slot numbers — reach the same verdict.

leader blockvotecertificate
  • Banded states that each verdict depends only on the blocks in a finite band of rounds above its slot.
  • Definition: for each verdict there is a round top such that any universe, view and schedule that agree with the original from the slot's round to top reach the same verdict. Agreement here means the same blocks, creators and references up to a shift of round numbers, the other view holding at least the original view's blocks in the band, and the same slot rounds, leaders and kinds up to a shift of slot numbers.
  • Left figure: rounds 2–5 of a Mysticeti DAG. Leader block 11 at round 3, votes 14–16 at round 4 (bracket 3 ≥ q) and certificates 17–19 at round 5 commit slot 1; the shaded band is rounds 3–5.
  • Right figure: the same DAG with rounds 0–1 cut and rounds shifted down by 2. The band is rounds 1–3, and block 11 commits slot 0. Both commits are checked on this DAG in Lean.
  • Since the other view may hold extra blocks in the band, a rule that decides on the absence of a block does not have Banded. Each of the eleven rules is proved to have it (slide 60).
  • Persistence under extension and invariance under a cut are derived from Banded (slide 57); the mechanisms that cut, fill or shift rounds and the safety theorem (slide 58) use it.

Agree, CommitsCandidate, Indirect

  • Agree: two views of one universe never decide a slot differently, skips included.
  • CommitsCandidate: a committed block is a candidate of its slot.
  • Indirect: a committed eligible anchor, with every eligible slot in between skipped, decides the slot; changing the other slots' leaders does not change that verdict.
  • Three further properties: verdicts agree across views, a commit names a real candidate, and a later committed anchor decides earlier slots.
  • Agree: under one schedule and over one universe, any two views that decide a slot reach the same verdict, a skip counted as a verdict. The safety theorem uses it.
  • CommitsCandidate: a committed block is a block of the universe, at the slot's round, by the slot's leader. It does not follow from Banded, which constrains which DAGs a verdict distinguishes and says nothing about what the committed identifier denotes. Safety, inclusion and chain quality use it.
  • Step 1: in the diagram, slot j holds a committed anchor that is eligible for slot i, where eligibility depends only on the rounds of the two slots; every eligible slot between them is skipped. Indirect states that slot i is then decided, with some verdict v.
  • Step 2: the second row is a schedule S′ with the same rounds and the same leader and kind at slot i, but other leaders elsewhere (blue). If slot j still commits the anchor and the slots between are still skipped under S′, slot i receives the same verdict v.
  • Each rule proves Indirect by cases on slot i's own candidate and the anchor's history, which a change of leaders elsewhere does not affect. From this stronger form, Descends is derived once (slide 57).

The support: the conditions for a commit

  • A support names the wave and what it means for a block to certify a candidate.
  • Law 1 (local): certification depends only on the wave's rounds, so it is unchanged by cutting or shifting rounds outside them.
  • Law 2 (commits): if a reliable quorum T leads a slot, produces through its wave and certifies every candidate, then a view that holds those rounds commits the slot.
  • Liveness uses this premise, live, at every slot T leads; the two network assumptions are used only to establish it.
  • A support describes what a rule's commit counts; two laws relate it to the rule's verdicts, and liveness is proved from them.
  • A support gives a wave length, the number of rounds between a candidate and its certifiers, and a relation stating when a block certifies a candidate. For Odontoceti, Nemo-Nemo and Hybrid the wave length is 1 and certification is a reference.
  • Law 1: across a cut or a shift that leaves the certifier's wave unchanged, a block certifies the same candidates as before.
  • Law 2, in the figure: T is a reliable quorum (bracket) that leads the slot of L (row v0), has a block at every round of the wave, and every T-block C at round r + wave certifies every candidate.
  • Step 1: a view that holds the rounds of the wave then commits the slot (badge commit L).
  • Step 2: the premise live requires this at every slot that T leads in a window, on a view that holds the window. Liveness uses only live.
  • Step 2: the lower diagram shows the two ways to establish live: from synchrony and coverage, by one theorem stated for every support, or from a reactive pacemaker execution, proved per rule. No synchrony assumption appears in the properties layer; a script checks this as part of the build.

Optional and derived properties

Optional, needed only by the mechanism named in parentheses:

  • CommitsDirect: a direct commit is a verdict (adaptive leader count).
  • SkipsUnsupported: a slot is skipped when a large enough set, present one round above, references none of its candidates (prompt skip).
  • Quorate: every block above genesis references blocks of n − f distinct creators (chain quality).
  • SelfParent, NoEquiv: every block references its creator's previous block; a reliable creator makes one block per round (inclusion).
  • Some properties are needed only by one mechanism; others are derived once from the core properties, so no rule has to prove them.
  • CommitsDirect: a candidate that passes the rule's direct-commit test is committed; adaptive leader count uses it. SkipsUnsupported: if a set of validators meeting the rule's size condition has blocks in the view one round above the slot and none of them references a candidate, the slot is skipped; prompt skip uses it.
  • Quorate: every non-genesis block references blocks of at least n − f distinct creators, under the standard fault model; chain quality uses it. SelfParent and NoEquiv: every non-genesis block references a block of its own creator, and a reliable creator has one block per round; inclusion uses them.
  • Step 1: in the diagram, Persist (a verdict survives extension of the universe and the view) and LocalTruncate (a replica that has pruned below a horizon reaches the same verdicts, at its own numbering) are derived from Banded.
  • Step 1: LeaderCommits (a slot led by a member of a reliable quorum is committed wherever live holds) is derived from Law 2, and Descends (below a run of consecutive committed slots, every slot is decided) is derived from Indirect.
  • Some rules also prove a derived property directly: Mysticeti proves LeaderCommits and derives Law 2 from it, and Steelhead proves persistence directly.

Safety, for every rule and every mechanism

From Banded, Agree and CommitsCandidate, across any sequence of cuts, recoveries and re-geneses:

  • every verdict above the settling round is the same before and after;
  • any view after agrees with any view before, above the settling round;
  • every commit is a candidate, and no block is committed at two slots;
  • adding blocks never changes a verdict.
  • The safety theorem: every rule with Banded, Agree and CommitsCandidate is safe across any composition of mechanisms that cut, fill or re-genesis the DAG. It is proved once, in Lean, for all eleven rules.
  • The settling round is the round from which the original and the transformed DAG hold the same blocks, up to a shift of round numbers; below it the mechanisms change the DAG.
  • In the diagram: the source DAG, the DAG after a fill (dashed blue: filled holes), and the DAG after a cut. The bottom row, verdicts of the slots above the settling round, is equal in all three.
  • The four conclusions: verdicts above the settling round are the same before and after, at the shifted slot numbers; any view after agrees with any view before above that round; every commit is a candidate, and no block is committed at two slots; and when blocks are added to the universe, a view and any larger view agree at every slot.
  • The ledger reading: two validators' decided prefixes above the settling round are equal. The next slide states liveness.

Liveness, for every rule

From Law 2, CommitsCandidate, SelfParent and NoEquiv:

  • Progress: every slot below a run of reliably led slots is decided, and reliably led slots continue to be committed.
  • Inclusion: every block of a reliable validator enters the ledger, through a later slot its creator leads.

Seven rules have both. Nemo-Nemo, FinWhale, Hydrozoan and Optimal-Hydrozoan lack SelfParent and have progress only.

  • The liveness theorem: from Law 2, CommitsCandidate, SelfParent and NoEquiv, a rule makes progress and includes every reliable validator's blocks, wherever the premise live holds.
  • Progress: if, past every point, the schedule has a run of consecutive slots led by members of a reliable quorum T, then every slot below such a run is decided, and slots led by T continue to be committed. Progress also assumes Descends, which is derived from Indirect.
  • Inclusion: under a schedule in which each reliable validator leads infinitely often, every block of a reliable validator enters the ledger.
  • Step 1: the diagram shows block b of a reliable validator v at round r; each later block of v references its predecessor (self-parent), up to the leader block of a later slot that v leads. When that slot is committed, b is in the leader block's history and enters the ledger. NoEquiv ensures that b is the only block of v at round r, so the chain passes through it.
  • Seven rules have both progress and inclusion. Nemo-Nemo, FinWhale, Hydrozoan and Optimal-Hydrozoan lack SelfParent and are proved to make progress only.

Which rule has which property

All eleven rules have Banded, Agree, CommitsCandidate, Indirect, CommitsDirect, and a support with both laws.

  • The table records which optional properties and which headline theorems each of the eleven rules has; the core properties hold for all of them.
  • The sentence above the table lists what all eleven have: Banded, Agree, CommitsCandidate, Indirect, CommitsDirect, and a support with both laws. In the table, ✓ means proved in Lean, and — means not proved here, which is a weaker statement than refuted.
  • The Safe column is complete, so the safety theorem of slide 58 applies to every rule. In the Lives column, the four rules without SelfParent have progress only.
  • Mahi-Mahi's theorems are proved for wave length w ≥ 2, as properties conditional on live; synchrony establishes live for Mahi-Mahi only when w ≥ 4, which is the bound on slide 50.
  • An optional property is needed only by its mechanism: prompt skip applies to the five rules with SkipsUnsupported, and chain quality to the ten rules with Quorate.

The properties a user sees

  • The table maps each guarantee a user observes to the properties or mechanisms that provide it.
  • The first two rows are the headline theorems: ledgers agree by the safety theorem, and every slot is eventually decided by progress, which uses Law 2 and, through Descends, Indirect.
  • A validator decides from the blocks it holds: this is proved for the pacemakers of Mysticeti and Bluestreak (slide 66).
  • Chain quality, that a committed block's history contains blocks of at least half of the correct validators, also requires that twice the slack be at most the number of correct validators. Inclusion of every correct validator's blocks uses SelfParent, NoEquiv, CommitsCandidate and LeaderCommits.
  • The two storage bounds are stated over the storage model rather than over the carrier: the novelty budget keeps storage linear under equivocation (slide 70), and garbage collection keeps it constant (slide 72).
Part IV

Mechanisms

The mechanisms

  • This slide lists the mechanisms of Part IV; each addresses a problem that the commit rule alone leaves open.
  • Each row gives the problem in the second column, the properties of the rule that the mechanism's proofs use in the third, and the slides that treat it in the last.
  • The properties in the “Uses” column are those defined on slides 54–57; the caption gives the slide for each.
  • The storage bound differs from the other rows: it is stated over the delivery of blocks and reads no property of the commit rule.
  • We begin with pacing: how a rule that only counts references makes progress in time.

Liveness, and the role of time

  • The commit rule counts references; it does not refer to time.
  • Liveness is reduced to two facts about the DAG, from some round on:
    • every reliable validator has a block in each round;
    • each reliable block references every reliable block of the round below.
  • These follow from view convergence and the pacemaker's rules.
Uses: view convergence and the pacemaker's rules (slide 64).
Gives: the support's precondition live (slide 56).
  • The commit rule counts references and does not refer to time, so the liveness argument is built in layers, and only the lower layers refer to time.
  • Read the diagram from top to bottom: each arrow is labelled with what the layer below receives. The network gives view convergence after GST, the global stabilisation time after which every block reaches every reliable validator within the delay Δ.
  • The pacemaker turns view convergence into two facts about the DAG, from some round on: every reliable validator has a block in each round, and each reliable block references every reliable block of the round below. The reliable validators are a set of at least quorum size that follows the pacemaker.
  • These two facts are the support's precondition live (slide 56), and Law 2 turns live into commits. For Mysticeti it is proved in Lean that the two facts give a reliable leader a certificate, and hence a direct commit.
  • The next slide states the pacemaker's four rules.

The pacemaker's rules

  • Advance: a validator holding blocks of n − f creators at round r moves past round r.
  • Catch up: after GST, a validator that holds a reliable block of round r enters round r within proc, the time to process and build a block.
  • Wait: a validator spends at least timeout(r) in round r.
  • Reference: a validator's block references every block of the previous round that it holds.
  • The pacemaker decides when a validator leaves a round; four rules govern it.
  • The diagram follows one validator's round counter from top to bottom; each arrow is labelled with the rule that governs it.
  • Catch up (top arrow): after GST, a validator that holds a reliable block of round r enters round r within proc, the time to process a block and build its own. Wait (the box “in round r”): it spends at least timeout(r) in round r.
  • Advance (middle arrow): a validator that holds blocks of n − f distinct creators at round r moves past round r. Reference: the block it then builds references every round-r block it holds.
  • Advance, with view convergence, gives every reliable validator a block in every round. Reference, with Wait and a large enough timeout, gives that each reliable block references every reliable block below. The next slide shows how large the timeout must be.

Drift collapses in one round

  • Validators' clocks may drift apart before GST.
  • After GST, catching up brings every reliable validator within Δ + proc of the others in one round, whatever the spread before.
  • A timeout of 2Δ + proc therefore suffices; it does not depend on the spread before GST.
  • Before GST the validators' round entry times may drift arbitrarily far apart; this slide shows that, at any round that every reliable validator enters after GST, the spread is at most Δ + proc.
  • In the chart the horizontal axis is the round and the vertical axis is each validator's entry time minus the earliest entry at that round. With GST = 12, Δ = 2, proc = 1, v3 enters round 0 ten units late, before GST; from round 1 it is 3 = Δ + proc late. v0 is Byzantine, and its line coincides with v1's.
  • The mechanism: after GST, the earliest validator's block reaches the last validator within Δ, and Catch up makes the last validator enter that round within proc. This is proved in Lean for any spread before GST.
  • Consequently a timeout of 2Δ + proc suffices for each reliable block to reference every reliable block below, and the bound has no term for the spread before GST. In the example the timeout is 5 = 2·2 + 1, and the decision of the slots is checked on the concrete DAG with no hypothesis on the spread.
  • The statement that waiting alone, without Catch up, does not reduce drift is informal: it has no Lean statement and is not proved.

The reactive schedule, and local liveness

  • A validator waits only until it holds the leader's block, then votes; the timeout is a fallback.
  • The vote round then takes at most drift + delivery + processing. When that sum is below the timeout, no timeout fires.
  • Every reliable validator decides from the blocks it holds, by an explicit time.
  • The reactive schedule shortens rounds: a validator waits only until it holds the leader's block, then votes, and the full timeout is a fallback.
  • In the table, validator v builds its round-r block at time v + 6r, so each validator spends 6 time units in every round. The chart plots this constant 6 against the timeout line at 9 = 2Δ + proc, with Δ = 2 and proc = 5.
  • Proved in Lean: when every reliable block of the leader's round reaches every reliable validator within δ of its creation, the round above is built within D + δ + proc of round entry, where D is the drift. When this sum is below the timeout, no timeout fires.
  • Local liveness: after GST, every reliable validator decides the slot from the blocks it holds itself, by an explicit time. This strengthens the earlier statement, which reads the whole DAG.
  • The reactive schedule gives up the guarantee that each reliable block references every reliable block of the round below. Inclusion of correct blocks, defined on the next slide, is still proved, along each validator's own chain once that validator leads a slot.

Chain quality

  • Coverage: the history of every committed block contains, at every round below it, blocks of at least |Correct| − f correct validators. No timing assumption is needed.
  • Inclusion: a correct validator's block is committed once a later slot it leads commits.
  • Coverage holds for every rule except Bluestreak. Inclusion holds for the seven rules with SelfParent and NoEquiv.
Uses: Quorate and CommitsCandidate (coverage); SelfParent, NoEquiv and LeaderCommits (inclusion).
Gives: lower bounds on which correct validators' blocks enter the ledger.
  • Chain quality concerns which validators' blocks enter the ledger; two properties give lower bounds.
  • Coverage: the history of a committed leader block, that is, the set of blocks it reaches by references, holds at every round below it blocks of at least |Correct| − f correct validators. It is proved for any view and with no timing assumption, from Quorate and CommitsCandidate.
  • In the figure n = 4, f = 1 and v0 is Byzantine, so |Correct| = 3. Slot 1 commits leader block 13; the shaded region is its history, and the brackets show the correct creators v1 and v2 at each of rounds 0–2, that is, 2 = |Correct| − f.
  • Inclusion: a correct validator's blocks form a chain, by SelfParent and NoEquiv, so a committed leader block of that validator reaches all its earlier blocks. With LeaderCommits and a schedule that returns to every correct validator, every correct block enters the ledger.
  • Coverage is proved for every rule except Bluestreak, for which Quorate is not shown; inclusion is proved for the seven rules with SelfParent and NoEquiv. The next slide shows that coverage alone does not give inclusion.

Coverage does not give inclusion

Validators 0, 1, 2 reference only each other for six rounds; validator 3 is correct and no other validator references it. Each round of block 13's history has 2 correct creators, exactly the bound |Correct| − f. None of validator 3's blocks enters the committed leader's history.

  • This slide shows a DAG in which coverage holds with equality and a correct validator's blocks are still absent from the ledger.
  • In the figure, validators 0, 1 and 2 reference only each other for six rounds. The marked blocks 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23 are validator 3's, and the drawn path is the only set of references to them: each is referenced only by validator 3's next block.
  • Slot 1 commits block 13. Each round of its history has exactly 2 correct creators, v1 and v2, which meets the bound |Correct| − f = 3 − 1.
  • Checked on this concrete DAG: no block of validator 3 is in slot 1's history, and block 7 is not in the ledger.
  • Coverage counts correct creators per round and does not determine which ones; inclusion therefore needs the separate argument along a validator's own chain from the previous slide.

Equivocation and exposure

  • Safety requires no restriction on equivocation; bounded storage does.
  • A creator is exposed in a block's history when the history holds two of its blocks in one round.
  • Rule: never reference a block whose creator is exposed in your own history.
  • This alone bounds a history, but with a constant that grows like f^f: one history can hold several chains of one creator (2^e chains with e = 2 in the figure).
Uses: no property of the rule; only which blocks a validator accepts.
Gives: a bound on what a correct validator stores (next slide).
  • Safety requires no restriction on equivocation, that is, on a validator creating two different blocks in one round; bounded storage does, and this slide introduces the restriction. The safety results are proved without it.
  • Step 1: a creator is exposed in a block's history when that history holds two of its blocks in one round. In the figure, block 41's history holds validator 2's twins 27 and 29 (red bracket), and the badge lists the two creators exposed in it, v1 and v2.
  • Step 1: the rule is that a block never references a block whose creator is exposed in the referencing block's own history. Every block of this DAG obeys it; this is checked on the concrete DAG.
  • Step 2: the rule alone bounds a history; proved in Lean, a block of round r has at most (n + (n − 1)·f^f)·(r + 1) blocks in its history. The constant grows like f^f.
  • Step 2: the figure shows why the constant is large. Block 41 exposes e = 2 creators, and the dark arrows from it reach 2^e = 4 round-0 blocks of v1 (1, 13, 14, 15), so its history holds four chains of one creator. This is checked at e = 2 on this DAG; the count 2^e for general e is not proved.
  • The bound uses no property of the commit rule, only which blocks a validator accepts. The next slide makes it linear in the round.

The novelty budget

  • Accept a block only if its history adds at most τ blocks you do not hold; reference only blocks you have accepted.
  • The rule is independent of a block's creator.
  • Storage then grows linearly: with C correct validators, a correct validator holds at most C·((1 + fτ)·r + 1 + f) blocks by round r. At C = 3, f = 1, τ = 3, round 9: 114 blocks.
  • The novelty budget makes storage grow linearly in the round, by limiting what one acceptance may add to a validator's store.
  • The novelty of a block, for a validator, is the set of blocks in its history that the validator does not hold. The rule: accept a block only if its novelty has at most τ blocks, and reference only accepted blocks. The rule does not depend on the block's creator, so a validator can enforce it without knowing which validators are Byzantine.
  • Proved in Lean, from round 0 and without timing assumptions: with C correct validators, a correct validator holds at most C·((1 + fτ)·r + 1 + f) blocks by round r.
  • The chart evaluates the bound at C = 3, f = 1, τ = 3: 12r + 6 blocks, from 6 at round 0 to 114 at round 9.
  • Also proved: once every correct block is delivered from some round on, a correct block's novelty is at most f·κ + 1, where κ bounds the novelty of an accepted Byzantine block.
  • The bound still grows with r; garbage collection, on the next slides, makes it constant.

The cut

  • Each validator keeps a horizon G and discards every block below it. Validators do not agree on G.
  • Keep the blocks of rounds ≥ G and renumber round G as round 0, with no references. The result is again a valid DAG.
  • Slot d + k of the full DAG and slot k of the cut DAG have the same verdict.
Uses: Banded, Agree, and Law 1 of the support. Gives: the same verdicts and liveness after the cut, and constant storage (next slide).
  • Garbage collection discards old blocks; the cut is the operation on the DAG that describes the result.
  • Each validator keeps a horizon G and discards every block below it; different validators may hold different horizons.
  • Step 1: in the left figure, G = 2; the faded blocks of rounds 0 and 1 are discarded.
  • Step 2: the right figure is the cut DAG. Rounds 2–5 are renumbered 0–3, and the round-2 blocks, such as block 8, become round-0 blocks with no references; the result is again a valid DAG.
  • Proved in Lean: when G is at most the round of slot d, slot d + k of the full DAG and slot k of the cut DAG have the same verdict, and validators with different horizons agree. In the figure d = 1: block 11 is committed by slot 1 before the cut and by slot 0 after it, checked on this DAG.
  • The proofs use Banded, Agree and Law 1, and give the same verdicts and liveness after the cut. The next slide bounds storage.

Storage is constant

With the horizon at most Λ rounds below the current round, a correct validator keeps at most C·(Λ + 1) + C·f + Λ·C·f·κ blocks, whatever the round. Here κ bounds the number of new blocks that accepting one Byzantine block adds to the store. At C = 3, f = 1, κ = 3, Λ = 5: 66 blocks.

  • With garbage collection, the bound on storage no longer depends on the current round.
  • Proved in Lean: when the horizon G lies at most Λ rounds below the current round t, a correct validator keeps at most C·(Λ + 1) + C·f + Λ·C·f·κ blocks, where C is the number of correct validators and κ bounds the new blocks that accepting one Byzantine block adds.
  • Step 1: at t = 5 the shaded rounds 0–5 are retained. Step 2: at t = 8, rounds 3–8. Step 3: at t = 11, rounds 6–11. The window moves with t, and the bound in the right column stays at 66.
  • At C = 3, f = 1, κ = 3, Λ = 5 the bound is 3·6 + 3·1 + 5·3·1·3 = 18 + 3 + 45 = 66.
  • The next slide treats a validator that starts with none of the discarded blocks.

Joining from an attested base

  • A new validator adopts a round-G block when blocks of at least f + 1 distinct creators at a later round t reach it.
  • One of those creators is correct, so every base block is attested by a correct validator. No signatures are needed.
  • It then copies a correct peer's blocks above G. Its verdicts equal those of any validator with the full history.
  • A new validator cannot obtain the discarded history; this slide shows how it chooses a starting layer at round G without trusting any single peer.
  • It adopts a round-G block when blocks of at least f + 1 distinct creators at a later round t reach it; the adopted blocks form the attested base. In the figure G = 1, t = 4, and the round-4 blocks 14, 15, 16 have three creators, 3 ≥ f + 1 = 2.
  • Step 1: among f + 1 creators at least one is correct, so every base block lies in the history of a correct validator's block, with no signatures required. Here the base is {5, 6, 7}, and every base block is reached from all three attesters; this is checked on the DAG.
  • Step 2: the validator then copies a correct peer's blocks above G, here 8, 9, 10, and holds blocks 5–10.
  • Step 2: proved in Lean: after the network synchronises, and when t is at least two rounds above the peer's latest round, the new validator's verdicts never conflict with those of any validator holding the full history.

Choosing the lag

An equivocation whose two blocks both fall below the cut is no longer detected.

  • This slide relates the distance between the horizon and the current round to the guarantees that hold.
  • Each bar shows where the horizon G may lie relative to the current round t; the table restates the bars.
  • Top bar: with G anywhere, safety holds; the agreement results for the cut, for different horizons and for a joining validator need no bound on G.
  • Middle bar: with G ≤ t − 1, after the network synchronises, every block a correct validator discards is already held by every correct peer one round later. Bottom bar: with G ≤ t − 2, every round-G block a correct validator accepted is in the attested base.
  • An equivocation whose two blocks both fall below the cut is no longer detected: on a concrete DAG, the equivocating creator is not exposed in a block's history after the cut. The cut preserves the storage rule of slide 69; this is proved in Lean.
  • The statement that a cut above an undecided slot leaves it undecided is informal and not proved.

Crash recovery: the message

  • A validator v₁ crashed after its block B₁ and returns at round r. It cannot create a block: a valid block needs its own previous block one round below.
  • It sends one message: B₁, r, a donor validator v₂, and fresh identifiers.
  • Every receiver computes a filled block for v₁ at each missed round: the donor's references and payload at that round, plus a reference to v₁'s previous block.
Uses: Banded (through Persist), Agree, SkipsUnsupported, Law 1. Gives: v₁ producing again, with every earlier verdict unchanged.
  • Crash recovery: a validator v₁ that missed rounds cannot create a block, because a valid block needs its creator's previous block one round below. In the left figure, v₁ = v3 stops after block 3, which is B₁.
  • Step 1: on its return at round r, it sends one message: B₁, r, a donor validator v₂, and fresh identifiers for the new blocks. In the right figure the donor is v1, with blocks 5, 9, 13, 17.
  • Step 2: every receiver computes a filled block for v₁ at each missed round: the donor's references and payload at that round, plus a reference to v₁'s previous block. These are the dashed blocks 21–24; block 21 references {3, 0, 1, 2}, that is, block 3 together with the references of donor block 5.
  • The proofs use Banded (through Persist), Agree, SkipsUnsupported and Law 1, and give v₁ producing again with every earlier verdict unchanged; the next slide lists the results.
  • The statement that rebuilding costs one round trip per missed round is informal and not proved.

What the fill guarantees

  1. The filled DAG is valid, and every old block is unchanged.
  2. v₁ has a block at every missed round, so it can produce again.
  3. A slot led by v₁ in the missed rounds is skipped at once, given a quorum one round above (the prompt skip). No later view can commit it.
  4. Every verdict reached before the fill agrees with every verdict after it.
  • This slide lists what the fill guarantees; each item is proved in Lean.
  • Step 1: the filled DAG is valid, and every old block is unchanged, so every store, view and certificate built on the old DAG reads the same data.
  • Step 2: v₁ has a block at every missed round, the shaded blocks 21–24 at rounds 1–4, which is the production fact that liveness requires.
  • Step 3: the prompt skip. A slot led by v₁ in the missed rounds has only filled blocks as candidates, and no old block references them; given a quorum of old blocks one round above, the slot is skipped at once (SkipsUnsupported), and with Agree and Banded no later view commits it. It is proved for Mysticeti, Odontoceti, Hybrid, Hydrozoan and Bluestreak.
  • Step 3: in this example the schedule places no slot led by v3 in rounds 1–4; the prompt skip is shown on slide 80.
  • Step 4: every verdict reached before the fill agrees with every verdict reached after it, from Persist and Agree.

Jumping rounds

  • A validator's own blocks form a chain, so the donor's whole line is fixed by its top block.
  • The fill depends only on B₁, the donor's top block B₂, and the fresh identifiers. The message carries these and the two validators v₁, v₂.
  • A receiver that holds B₂ holds the donor's whole line. After the one message, v₁ has a block at every round up to B₂'s round, so it can produce at the next.
  • One message suffices for any number of missed rounds, because the donor's line of blocks is determined by its top block.
  • In the diagram the top row is the donor v1's line and the bottom row is v3's: B₁ = 3 and the filled blocks 21–24. Dashed arrows show which donor block each filled block copies its references from; green arrows are self-references.
  • A validator's own blocks form a chain, so from B₂ = 17 the previous own blocks 13, 9, 5 follow. Proved in Lean: the fill depends only on B₁, B₂ and the fresh identifiers, so the message carries these and v₁, v₂.
  • A receiver that holds B₂ holds the donor's whole line, since a view contains the history of each of its blocks. After the one message, v₁ has a block at every round up to round 4, the round of B₂, and can produce at round 5.
  • The statement that the message has constant size is informal: the fresh identifiers are modelled as a supply, and no size bound is proved.

Limits of the fill

  • With the horizon Λ rounds below the current round, one message recovers from an outage of at most Λ rounds.
  • After a longer outage, B₁ has been discarded.
  • No old block references a filled block, so v₁ is not covered in the rounds it missed.
  • The storage rule must be re-checked; with a donor line whose blocks all reach B₁, and v₁ not equivocating, it is one reachability check per round.
  • If the donor line is taken from blocks every receiver already holds, nothing else needs to be sent.
  • This slide states the limits of the fill.
  • Step 1: with the horizon Λ rounds below the current round, one message recovers from an outage of at most Λ rounds; proved in Lean, B₁ is retained exactly when the outage is at most Λ. In the figure r = 10, Λ = 5, rounds 5–10 are retained, and B₁ at round 5 is reached.
  • Step 2: after a 6-round outage, B₁ at round 4 has been discarded, and v₁ has no block in the cut DAG; the next slide treats this case.
  • Step 3: no old block references a filled block, so if v₁ is counted as reliable, the property that every reliable block references every reliable block of the round below fails at the missed rounds. With v₁ excluded, that property is unchanged.
  • Step 3: the storage rule must be re-checked for the filled blocks. Proved: if each donor block reaches B₁ and v₁ never equivocated, the filled DAG satisfies the rule, so the check is one reachability test per round.
  • Step 3: if the donor line is one that every receiver holds, every copied reference lies in the history of every block two rounds above it, so nothing beyond the message is sent; the self-reference is to v₁'s own block.

Re-genesis: recovering after a long outage

  • If all of v₁'s blocks are below the horizon, its chain of own blocks cannot be continued.
  • Each validator adds a round-0 block for v₁, with no references, to its cut DAG. This needs no exception to the self-parent rule.
  • Procedure: (1) join from the attested base to read; (2) re-genesis to write; (3) one fill message from the genesis block to the current round.
  • While a quorum still produces blocks, at most f validators can be in this state at once.
Uses: Banded, Agree, Law 1, and the attested base (slide 73). Gives: a validator back in production after any outage.
  • Re-genesis recovers a validator v₁ all of whose blocks are below the horizon. Proved in Lean: a validator with no round-0 block in a DAG has no block in it at all, since every block's chain of own blocks descends to round 0.
  • Step 1: each validator adds a round-0 block for v₁, with no references, to its cut DAG; round-0 blocks have no references, so no exception to the self-parent rule is needed. In the figure this is block 999. Proved in Lean: adding the block preserves every verdict and the storage rule.
  • Step 1: the statement that each validator derives this block locally, without it being transmitted, is informal; what is proved is that a later cut removes it.
  • Step 2: the procedure is (1) join from the attested base of slide 73 to read the DAG, (2) re-genesis to be able to write, (3) one fill message from the genesis block to the current round. In the figure the filled block 1001 has the references of donor block 9, blocks 4, 5, 6, and references 999; this is checked on the concrete DAG.
  • Step 2: while a quorum produces blocks, at most f validators can be without blocks at once, since a producing set of quorum size contains none of them.
  • The proofs use Banded, Agree, Law 1 and the attested base, and give a validator back in production after an outage of any length.

The chain fill (Bluestreak)

  • Copying a donor's references would attribute to v₁ claims it never made.
  • Each filled block references only v₁'s previous block and carries no tag and no claim. The message is v₁, B₁, r and fresh identifiers; it names no donor.
  • Verdicts do not change: slot 2 is committed and slot 3 skipped, before and after.
Uses: the same properties as the fill, and Bluestreak's claim discipline.
Gives: recovery for a rule whose blocks carry claims.
  • Bluestreak's blocks carry claims, and the donor fill would attribute to v₁ claims it never made; this motivation is informal and not proved.
  • The chain fill: each filled block references only v₁'s previous block and carries no leader tag and no claim. The message is v₁, B₁, r and fresh identifiers, and names no donor.
  • In the figure n = 4, f = 1, v0 is Byzantine and slot k is at round k. Validator 3 is correct and silent from round 2; B₁ = 7, and the filled blocks 102 and 103 chain back to it. The claim arrows point to the leader blocks 5 and 10.
  • Checked on this DAG: slot 2 commits block 10 and slot 3 is skipped, before and after the fill. After the fill, slot 3's candidate is block 103, which no round-4 block references; with the quorum {0, 1, 2} present at round 4 it is skipped at once, the prompt skip of slide 76.
  • Proved in Lean: when the filled blocks claim nothing, Bluestreak's claim discipline holds after the chain fill. With the properties used by the fill, this gives recovery for a rule whose blocks carry claims.

Every mechanism is one relation

Each mechanism relates the DAG it reads to the DAG it writes: the same blocks from a settling round on, renumbered by G rounds, with the same creators and payloads, and the same references strictly above the settling round.

  • A cut is such a relation; so are a fill and a re-genesis (with G = 0).
  • A sequence of them is again one: the composite keeps the same blocks from the later settling round on.
Uses: Banded, Agree, Law 1.
Gives: safety and liveness for any combination of cuts, fills and re-geneses (next slide).
  • This slide shows that a cut, a fill and a re-genesis are instances of one relation between the DAG a mechanism reads and the DAG it writes, and that a sequence of them is again an instance.
  • The relation has an offset G and a settling round. From the settling round on, the written DAG holds the same blocks at rounds lowered by G, with the same creators and payloads, and with the same references strictly above the settling round; below the settling round the relation says nothing.
  • The rows of the figure are drawn at D's rounds 0–20. In the top row, D lacks validator v₁'s blocks at rounds 6–10.
  • Step 1: a fill with r = 10 adds those blocks. It has offset 0 and settles at round r + 1 = 11; a re-genesis is also a relation with G = 0.
  • Step 2: a cut at G = 15 drops rounds 0–14 and renumbers rounds 15–20 as 0–5. It settles at round 15.
  • Step 3: the composite of the fill and the cut is again one relation; it settles at max(r + 1, G) = 15, and the shaded rounds 15–20 hold the same blocks in all three rows. That a finite sequence of such relations is one relation is proved in Lean.
  • The next slide uses Banded, Agree and Law 1 to show what this gives: safety and liveness for every combination of cuts, fills and re-geneses.

Safe and live across any stack

From Banded, Agree and Law 1: across any stack, verdicts above the settling round are preserved, views agree, and the liveness precondition is preserved.
The cut, fill and re-genesis are each built once, and serve all eleven rules.

  • For any rule with Banded, Agree and a support, every stack of cuts, fills and re-geneses preserves safety and liveness above the composite settling round; this is proved in Lean.
  • A stack is a finite sequence of mechanisms. The theorem has three conclusions: a verdict at a slot above the settling round is the same before and after the stack, at the renumbered slot; any view of the result agrees with the original view on those verdicts; and the liveness precondition of the support carries over to the renumbered slots.
  • The table has one row per rule and one column per mechanism: ✓ means proved for that rule, and — means not shown.
  • The cut, the fill and the re-genesis are each built once, on a common record of the DAG; every rule reads its universes as that record, so each gets all three by one instance and no new proof.
  • The prompt skip is ticked for the five rules with SkipsUnsupported. Coverage and inclusion are the two halves of chain quality (slide 67): coverage is shown for every rule except Bluestreak, and inclusion is ticked for the seven rules with SelfParent and NoEquiv.
  • The next slides turn to a mechanism that changes the leader schedule itself.

Leaders chosen from the committed prefix

  • A fixed schedule may continue to name a crashed leader.
  • A configuration fixes the leaders of each round and an interval.
  • It decides up to its anchor (the first committed slot more than one interval past its start).
  • It outputs only up to its boundary.
  • The next configuration is computed from the anchor's history and the verdicts just output.
Uses: Agree (safety); Law 2 and Indirect (liveness).
Gives: a schedule every validator computes the same way.
  • Adaptive leaders replace a fixed leader schedule by a sequence of configurations, each computed from what has already been committed.
  • The motivation, that a fixed schedule may continue to name a crashed leader, is an informal argument and is not proved.
  • A configuration fixes the leaders of each round and an interval, the number of rounds before the next reconfiguration is due. In the figure each row is one configuration, with one leader per round and interval one, so a slot is a round.
  • Step 1: configuration 0 starts at round 0. Its anchor is the first committed slot whose round is more than one interval past the start: slot 2 is skipped, so the anchor is slot 3, which commits block 15. The configuration decides every slot up to its anchor.
  • Step 2: it outputs only the slots up to its boundary at round start + interval = 1, so the shaded output is [5].
  • Step 3: configuration 1 is computed from the anchor's history and the verdicts just output; it decides slot 3 again as 15 and outputs [ ], and configuration 2 outputs [15].
  • Safety uses Agree, and liveness uses Law 2 and Indirect; the next slide states the safety result.

Safe for every anchored score

  • Two validators that start from the same configuration agree on every configuration and every verdict.
  • The theorem assumes no timing, fairness or window, and holds for every score that reads the view only through the anchor's history.
  • For liveness the score must continue to assign reliable validators runs of consecutive slots.
  • Two validators that start from the same configuration agree on every later configuration, anchor and verdict, for every anchored update rule; this is proved in Lean.
  • An update rule is anchored when it returns the same configuration on any two views of one DAG, given the same anchor and the same verdicts. A score that reads the view only through the anchor's causal history is anchored.
  • The top row is validator a on view V, with configurations C₀, C₁, C₂ linked by the update. Step 1: validator b on view V′ starts from the same C₀.
  • Step 2: the vertical links state the theorem segment by segment: equal anchors and verdicts for C₀, and C₁ = C₁′, C₂ = C₂′ with equal anchors and verdicts, for every configuration both validators have reached.
  • The only property of the base rule the theorem uses is Agree; it assumes no timing, fairness or window.
  • Liveness is proved under further conditions on the score: it keeps the number of slots per round and the interval, and the configurations it produces continue to give reliable validators runs of consecutive slots. The next slide asks what a score may read when a mechanism adds or removes blocks.

What a score may read

  • A score that reads only the anchor's history is unaffected by crash recovery.
  • Under garbage collection the score must read verdicts relative to the configuration.
  • A score that names an absolute slot number gives different answers before and after a cut.
  • Crash recovery and garbage collection each restrict what a score may read.
  • Crash recovery, by a fill or a re-genesis, only adds blocks. A score that reads only the anchor's history returns the same configuration before and after; this is proved in Lean and checked for a concrete score.
  • Garbage collection cuts the DAG at a horizon G, and a joiner numbers its slots from the cut. The score must then be horizon-stable: on views that agree above G, the joiner's configuration is the network's with the rounds below G dropped. A score that only relabels leaders is horizon-stable at every cut.
  • In the figure the cut is at G = 1. The top row is the network, with slots numbered from round 0; the bottom row is the joiner, whose slots 1 and 2 are the network's slots 2 and 3, with the same verdicts.
  • Step 1: the score shown swaps two leaders when slot 1 committed block 5. The network reads its slot 1, sees commit 5 and swaps; the joiner reads its own slot 1, sees no commit and keeps the leaders. Checked on a concrete DAG, this score is not horizon-stable at G = 1.
  • A score that reads verdicts must therefore read them relative to the configuration it closes. The next mechanism uses the same anchors to change the number of leaders per round.

The adaptive leader count

More leaders per round lower latency, but one slow leader delays every later slot. At each anchor:

  1. count the directly committed slots in the anchor's history;
  2. healthy if num · expected ≤ den · observed;
  3. healthy: one more leader; unhealthy: 2^backoff fewer, between 1 and maxLeaders; the backoff resets when healthy and grows otherwise.
Uses: Agree, CommitsCandidate, CommitsDirect (the count reads direct commits).
Gives: a leader count every validator computes the same way.
  • The adaptive leader count changes the number of leaders per round at each anchor, by additive increase and multiplicative decrease (AIMD).
  • The motivation, that more leaders lower latency and that one slow leader delays every later slot, is an informal argument and is not proved.
  • observed is the number of slots in the window of interval + 1 rounds up to the anchor's round that are directly committed in the anchor's history. expected is the number of slots in the rounds of that window old enough to have been decided; at one width m it is (interval − waveLength + 1)·m. The window is healthy if num · expected ≤ den · observed.
  • A healthy window adds one leader and resets the backoff to 0; an unhealthy window removes 2^backoff leaders and increases the backoff by one. The count is kept between 1 and maxLeaders.
  • The DAG figure: interval 4, one leader per round, anchor 21 at round 5. In the anchor's history only the leaders 5 and 10 are directly committed, so observed = 2 = expected, the window is healthy, and the next configuration has two leaders per round. This is checked on the concrete DAG.
  • Step 1: the chart follows five windows, healthy, healthy, unhealthy, unhealthy, healthy. The count goes 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2 with backoff 0, 0, 0, 1, 2 before each window; maxLeaders = 4 is not reached. The sequence is checked by computation in Lean.
  • The rule uses Agree, CommitsCandidate and CommitsDirect; CommitsDirect makes every slot counted as directly committed a committed slot.

Checkpoints

  • Correct online validators sign the checkpoint their deterministic state machine reaches after each commit in their own view, and witness certificates for what they signed.
  • A checkpoint certificate is at least q signatures on one proposal; a finality certificate is at least q witnesses of one.
  • Two checkpoint certificates at one epoch and height agree.
  • A correctly led slot, with production and certification, is finalised.
  • At an epoch change, the highest validated checkpoint becomes the next epoch's genesis.
Uses: Agree, CommitsCandidate, Law 2.
Gives: finalised application state, and its recovery across epochs.
  • Checkpoints turn the committed sequence into certified application state, and carry that state from one epoch to the next.
  • Read the figure from left to right. A correct online validator applies each commit in its own view to a deterministic state machine and signs the checkpoint it reaches; at least q signatures on one proposal form a checkpoint certificate. Each validator then witnesses the certificate for what it signed, and at least q witnesses form a finality certificate.
  • Safety: two checkpoint certificates at one epoch and height have the same content. Their quorums share a reliable signer, and that signer signs one state per height. This holds within one epoch and is proved in Lean.
  • Liveness: a slot with a correct leader, under the production and certification conditions, is finalised; this is also proved.
  • Step 1: at an epoch change, certificates of epoch e are broadcast, and the highest validated checkpoint becomes the genesis of epoch e + 1. The broadcast is assumed, not modelled (slide 89).
  • The construction uses Agree, CommitsCandidate and Law 2, and is instantiated for Hybrid and for the adaptive-leader runs.

Red Snapper: a fast path for owned objects

  • Validators state a stance on each object version inside their ordinary blocks; certificates for transactions, skips and unlocks are read from the DAG.
  • At n ≥ 3f + 1, uncontested transactions are decided from the DAG (fast quorum).
  • Conflicts are resolved at a committed anchor.
  • At n ≥ 5f + 1, a validator may change its vote on 2f + 1 opposing votes, coordinated by a coin.
  • Among any n − f votes on two sides, the larger side always has at least 2f + 1 exactly when n ≥ 5f + 1. The 5f + 1 certificate lemmas themselves need only n ≥ 3f + 1.
Uses: only the committed anchor sequence of the underlying consensus.
Gives: commits of owned-object transactions without waiting for consensus, except under conflict.
  • Red Snapper is a fast path for transactions on owned objects, run inside the ordinary DAG blocks; it uses only the committed anchor sequence of the underlying consensus.
  • Each block states a stance on each object version: an ACK of one transaction or ⊥. A certificate is a block whose references hold enough stances: n − f ACKs for a transaction certificate, 2f + 1 ⊥ votes for a skip or unlock certificate.
  • Left figure: n = 4, validator 0 is Byzantine (shaded) and has no blocks after round 0. Block 4 carries and ACKs the transaction, blocks 7, 8 and 9 ACK it, and each round-3 block 10, 11, 12 is a certificate over 3 ACKs (q = 3). The three certificates form a fast quorum, and the transaction is final with no anchor yet; this is checked on the concrete DAG.
  • Step 1, right figure: two conflicting transactions on one object. Every correct block declares ⊥, each correct round-3 block is an unlock certificate, and the committed anchor 12 releases the object and drops both transactions.
  • At n ≥ 5f + 1 a validator may change its vote on 2f + 1 opposing votes, coordinated by a coin. It is proved that among any n − f votes the larger side reaches 2f + 1 exactly when n ≥ 5f + 1; the certificate safety lemmas of that protocol are proved at n ≥ 3f + 1.
  • The result: owned-object transactions commit without waiting for consensus, except under conflict.

Open work

  • Adaptive leaders are proved generically; no rule has its own instance yet, and no concrete score that gives one validator several positions of the cycle is shown live.
  • Barbouni (proposed): change the schedule only at verdicts already decided.
  • Checkpoints: the broadcast algorithm is assumed, not modelled.
  • This slide lists what the development does not yet prove.
  • Adaptive leaders: safety and liveness are proved for any rule with the required properties, but no rule has its own adaptive instance. The two concrete scores in the deck are shown live because each produces a permutation of the rotation; a score that gives one validator several positions of the cycle is not shown live.
  • Barbouni is a proposal, described in the documentation only: it would change the schedule only at verdicts already decided. Nothing about it is proved.
  • Checkpoints: the authenticated broadcast at an epoch change is an assumed contract, not a modelled algorithm.

The development

  • LeanDag/Common/: blocks, the decision relation, ledgers.
  • LeanDag/Mysticeti/, LeanDag/Nemo/, …: one directory per rule.
  • LeanDag/Properties/: the properties and the safety and liveness headlines.
  • LeanDag/GC/, SafeSkip/, Reactive/, DoS/, Adaptive/, Barnacle/, Checkpoint/, RedSnapper/, Integration/: the mechanisms.
  • LeanDagTest/: every witness in this deck.
  • docs/report.md: the full written account.
  • This slide maps the repository onto the parts of the deck.
  • LeanDag/Common/ holds blocks, the decision relation and ledgers (Part I); one directory per rule, from Mysticeti/ to Steelhead/, holds the protocols (Part II); Properties/ holds the properties and the safety and liveness theorems (Part III).
  • GC/, SafeSkip/, Reactive/, DoS/, Adaptive/, Barnacle/, Checkpoint/, RedSnapper/ and Integration/ hold the mechanisms of Part IV.
  • LeanDagTest/ holds the concrete DAG behind every figure in the deck, and docs/report.md is the full written account.
  • One build checks the library and the witnesses. The axioms of every headline theorem are printed in the test files, and they are Lean's standard three: propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

Summary

  • One decision relation; eleven rules proved, two refuted.
  • Four properties and a support per rule; every mechanism proved once against them.
  • Safety with no network assumption; liveness from view convergence.
  • The summary fills in the three columns of slide 2: each rule proves the properties, and each mechanism uses them.
  • Left column: one decision relation, eleven rules proved, and two, Minnow and Black Marlin, refuted.
  • Middle column: four properties, Banded, Agree, CommitsCandidate and Indirect, and a support per rule with Law 1 and Law 2.
  • Right column: each mechanism is proved once against those properties; the pacemaker is per rule, and Red Snapper uses only the anchors.
  • Safety holds with no network assumption; liveness follows from view convergence.
  • Open: adaptive-leader instances for particular rules, Barbouni, and a model of the checkpoint broadcast (slide 89).
